title: Persian grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is standard Iranian Persian, the Persian that is written and read aloud, with a reading in Latin letters that shows the vowels Persian doesn't write: â as in “father”, a as in “cat”, e as in “bed”, o as in “go”, i as in “see”, u as in “food”; kh and gh are said in the throat, ' is a catch in the voice, and a hyphen marks the small gap inside a Persian word and the ezafe, the little -e that joins words.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Persian conversation.
lessons.topic: {{من}} “I”, {{تو}} and {{شما}} “you”; {{هستم}}, {{هستی}}, {{هستید}} “am, are”; the verb at the end

goal.t: سلام، من سارا هستم. اهل کانادا هستم.
goal.r: salâm, man sârâ hastam. ahl-e kânâdâ hastam.
goal.tr: Hello, I'm Sara. I'm from Canada.

dialog.tr: Hello! I'm Karim.
Hi, I'm Sara.
Where are you from?
I'm from Canada. And you?
I'm from Iran.
Nice to meet you!

blocks.p: **The verb comes last.** Look at where {{هستم|hastam}} “am” goes: at the very end. {{من سارا هستم.|man sârâ hastam.}} is, word for word, “I Sara am”. Almost every Persian sentence ends with its verb, so the end is where to listen for what is happening.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Canada.
a word for doing or being: am, go, eat, want. In Persian it comes at the end of the sentence.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{من|man}} is “I”. For “you” there are two words: {{تو|to}} for a friend, a child or family, and {{شما|shomâ}} for anyone else, and for more than one person. When in doubt, say {{شما}}: it is polite and never wrong. The end of the verb follows the pronoun: -am for “I”, -i for {{تو}}, -id for {{شما}}.

table: to a friend, a child, family
to anyone else (polite), or to several people

blocks.p: **Where from?** {{اهل|ahl}} means “from”, for where a person belongs: {{اهل ایران هستم.|ahl-e irân hastam.}} “I'm from Iran.” The short -e after it in the reading is the **ezafe**, a little sound that joins words together. Persian doesn't write it; lesson 3 is all about it.

ex.tr: I'm a student.
ex.note: no word for “a”: {{دانشجو|dâneshju}} is “student” or “a student”

ex.tr: Are you from Iran?
ex.note: a question just by raising your voice at the end

ex.tr: My name is Karim.
ex.note: {{است|ast}} is “is”; word for word “name-of me Karim is”

ex.tr: I'm from here.
Nice to meet you.
ex.note: said when you meet someone; word for word “I'm fortunate”

blocks.tip: Persian is written from right to left, and its short vowels (a, e, o) aren't written: {{من|man}} is just the letters m and n. The reading in Latin letters gives every vowel, and tapping an example lets you hear it. In the reading, â is the long a of “father”, a the short a of “cat”.
{{سلام|salâm}} is “hello” at any time of day, to anyone.

mistakes.why: The verb goes at the end: “I Sara am”.
With {{شما}} the verb ends in -id: {{هستید}}. ({{هستی}} goes with {{تو}}.)

practice.q: You're meeting your new teacher. “You” is…
practice.why: {{شما|shomâ}} is the polite “you”: use it with anyone you don't know well.

practice.tr: I'm from Canada.

practice.q: You're Sam, from England. Choose your replies.

About yourself: {{هستم}}. ({{هستید}} would be “you are”.)

practice.tr: I'm a student.

Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{سلام، من…}}

answers.r: salâm, man mâykel hastam. ahl-e âmrikâ hastam.

lessons.title: Point at things and name them
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?”, and say what something is and what it isn't.
lessons.topic: {{این}} “this” and {{آن}} “that”; {{است}} “is” and {{نیست}} “isn't”; nouns without “a” or “the”

goal.t: این چیست؟ این یک هدیه است.
goal.r: in chist? in yek hedye ast.
goal.tr: What's this? It's a present.

dialog.tr: What's this?
This is tea.

dialog.t: و آن چیست؟ آن هم چای است؟
dialog.r: va ân chist? ân ham chây ast?
dialog.tr: And what's that? Is that tea too?

dialog.t: نه، آن چای نیست. آن قهوه است.
dialog.r: na, ân chây nist. ân ghahve ast.
dialog.tr: No, that isn't tea. That's coffee.
Coffee? Great!

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{این|in}} is “this”, for something near you; {{آن|ân}} is “that”, further away. The thing comes next, and {{است|ast}} “is” at the end: {{این چای است.|in chây ast.}} “This is tea.”

blocks.means: a word for a person, a place or a thing: tea, book, Tehran, friend.

blocks.p: **No “the”, and no “he” or “she” for things.** {{کتاب|ketâb}} is “book”, “a book” and “the book”: the situation tells you which. For “a” you can add {{یک|yek}} “one”: {{این یک کتاب است.|in yek ketâb ast.}} “This is a book.” And Persian has no masculine and feminine: nothing ever changes to agree with a word.
**What is it?** {{چه|che}} “what” and {{است}} join into one word, {{چیست|chist}} “what is”: {{این چیست؟|in chist?}} “What's this?”. The answer goes in its place: {{این چای است.}}

**Not.** “Isn't” is a word of its own, {{نیست|nist}}, in the place of {{است}}: {{این قهوه نیست.|in ghahve nist.}} “This isn't coffee.” “I'm not” is {{نیستم|nistam}}, with the same endings as {{هستم}}.

ex.tr: This is a book.
That's a university.
This isn't water.
What's that?
Who's this?
ex.note: {{کی|ki}} “who” + {{است}}: about a person in a photo, for example

ex.tr: I'm not a student.

blocks.tip: In everyday speech {{است}} often shrinks to a short -e: you'll hear {{این چیه؟|in chiye?}} for {{این چیست؟}}. This course writes the standard {{است}}, which is also what you see written.

mistakes.why: {{است}} “is” goes at the end.
“Isn't” is one word, {{نیست}}, in the place of {{است}}.

practice.q: The cup you mean is far away, on another table. “That” is…
practice.why: {{آن|ân}} is “that”, further away; {{این|in}} is “this”, near you.

practice.tr: This isn't tea, it's coffee.

practice.q: A friend is showing you around. Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{چیست}} already has “is” in it, and it goes at the end.
{{نیستم}} is “I'm not”: you'd be saying “I'm not a library!”

practice.tr: That isn't water.

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say “a big city”, “the city is big” and “I'm tired”, with Persian's most important little sound: the ezafe.
lessons.topic: the ezafe (-e) between a noun and its adjective; adjective + {{است}}; the short “am, are”: {{خسته‌ام}}

goal.t: تهران یک شهر بزرگ است.
goal.r: tehrân yek shahr-e bozorg ast.
goal.tr: Tehran is a big city.

dialog.tr: Is the new house nice?

dialog.t: بله، خیلی خوب است. یک خانهٔ کوچک ولی قشنگ است.
dialog.r: bale, kheyli khub ast. yek khâne-ye kuchak vali ghashang ast.
dialog.tr: Yes, it's very nice. It's a small but pretty house.
How's the city?

dialog.t: شهر بزرگ و شلوغ است، ولی خیلی زیباست.
dialog.r: shahr bozorg va sholugh ast, vali kheyli zibâst.
dialog.tr: The city is big and busy, but it's very beautiful.
And you? Are you OK?
I'm fine, but I'm very tired!

blocks.p: **Two ways to describe.** Compare {{شهر بزرگ است.|shahr bozorg ast.}} “The city is big.” with {{یک شهر بزرگ|yek shahr-e bozorg}} “a big city”. In the first, the describing word comes before {{است}} “is”, as in English. In the second, it comes **after** the noun, joined to it by a short **-e**: shahr-e bozorg, “city-of big”.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, new, tired, Iranian.
the short -e (after a vowel, -ye) that joins a Persian noun to the word after it, the one that describes it or owns it: {{شهر بزرگ|shahr-e bozorg}} “a big city”. The word means “adding”.

blocks.p: **You hear the ezafe, but you usually don't see it.** After a consonant it isn't written at all: the reading shows it. After a vowel it becomes -ye and is written: as a small mark on a final {{ه}} ({{خانهٔ بزرگ|khâne-ye bozorg}} “a big house”) and as {{ی}} after {{ا}} or {{و}} ({{هوای خوب|havâ-ye khub}} “good weather”). More than one adjective? One more -e each time: {{یک ماشین قرمز قشنگ|yek mâshin-e ghermez-e ghashang}} “a pretty red car”.

table: a big city, the big city

blocks.p: **He or she.** {{او|u}} is both “he” and “she”: {{او خیلی مهربان است.|u kheyli mehrabân ast.}} is “He's very kind” or “She's very kind”.

blocks.means: a piece added to the end of a word that changes what it says: the -am of {{خسته‌ام|khaste-am}} “I'm tired”.

blocks.p: **I'm tired, you're well.** “Am” and “are” also have short forms: endings that hang on the describing word. {{خسته‌ام|khaste-am}} “I'm tired”, {{خوبی؟|khubi?}} “are you well?”. They are the endings of {{هستم}}, {{هستی}}… without the {{هست}}. For “he, she, it is”, keep {{است}}. After a final {{ه}} a small gap comes before the ending (the hyphen in the reading).

ex.tr: A hot coffee, please.
This is an Iranian film.
The new book is very good.
It's very cold.
ex.note: word for word “the air is very cold”

ex.tr: I'm very tired.
They're very kind.

blocks.tip: {{خیلی|kheyli}} “very” goes before the adjective, as in English: {{خیلی خوب|kheyli khub}} “very good”.

mistakes.why: The adjective comes after the noun, joined by -e: shahr-e bozorg.
Without {{است}} it is only “this good book”: a sentence needs its verb.

practice.q: Which one is a whole sentence: “The car is red”?
practice.why: With {{است}} it says something: “The car is red.” With the -e and no verb it is just “a red car”.

practice.tr: I'm very tired.
practice.why: “I am” is the ending -am: {{خسته‌ام}}. ({{خسته است}} is “he or she is tired”.)

options: یک بزرگ و زیبا شهر است.

lessons.title: Say whose it is
lessons.summary: Say “my name”, “Sara's bag” and “your phone”, with the ezafe and the little endings for “my, your, his”.
lessons.topic: the ezafe with an owner: {{کیف سارا|kif-e sârâ}}; the possessive endings -am, -at, -ash, -emân, -etân, -eshân

goal.t: اسم من مریم است. اسم شما چیست؟
goal.r: esm-e man maryam ast. esm-e shomâ chist?
goal.tr: My name is Maryam. What's your name?

dialog.tr: Excuse me, is this your bag?

dialog.t: نه، کیفم آبی است. این کیف دوستم است.
dialog.r: na, kifam âbi ast. in kif-e dustam ast.
dialog.tr: No, my bag is blue. This is my friend's bag.
Where's your friend?
Over there. Neda! Your bag!
Oh, thank you!

blocks.p: **Whose? The ezafe again.** The owner comes after the thing, joined by the same -e as an adjective: {{کیف سارا|kif-e sârâ}} “Sara's bag” (“bag-of Sara”), {{اسم من|esm-e man}} “my name” (“name-of me”), {{خانهٔ شما|khâne-ye shomâ}} “your house”.

blocks.means: a word or an ending that says whose something is: my, your, Sara's.

blocks.p: **Or a short ending.** “My”, “your”, “his” can also be endings on the thing: {{کیفم|kifam}} “my bag”, {{کیفت|kifat}} “your bag”, {{کیفش|kifash}} “his bag” or “her bag”. Both ways are right: {{اسم من}} and {{اسمم|esmam}} both mean “my name”. The endings are shorter, and everyday speech uses them most.

**A thing, its adjective and its owner:** the adjective first, then the owner, all joined with -e: {{کیف آبی من|kif-e âbi-ye man}} “my blue bag”; or with the ending on the last word: {{کیف آبی‌ام|kif-e âbi-am}}.

ex.tr: What's your name?
ex.note: to a friend; to anyone else, {{اسمتان چیست؟|esmetân chist?}}

ex.tr: This is my father's house.
Sara's bag is red.
His car is very old.
How are you?
ex.note: the polite everyday greeting; word for word “how is your state?”

ex.tr: My friend is from Shiraz.

mistakes.why: The owner comes after the thing: “bag-of me”, kif-e man.
Either {{اسم من}} or {{اسمم}}, not both: the ending already says “my”.

practice.why: {{ـش|-ash}} is “his” or “her”: Persian doesn't say which.

practice.tr: What's your name? (polite)
practice.why: “Your”, politely, is {{شما}} after the ezafe: esm-e shomâ.

practice.tr: This is my father's house.

practice.q: In a café, someone points at a phone on your table. Choose your reply.

lines.tr: Excuse me, is this your phone?

lines.why: “My phone” is {{گوشی من}}: the owner after the thing. ({{من گوشی است}} says “I is a phone”!)

practice.tr: This isn't my bag.

practice.q: Say “my new car”, with the ending for “my”.
Your turn: introduce someone in your family or a friend: their name and one thing about them. Use {{اسمش…}} or {{اسم … من}}.

answers.r: in barâdaram ast. esmash ali ast.
answers.tr: This is my brother. His name is Ali.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask where, what, who, when, how and why, and ask yes-or-no questions, the Persian way.
lessons.topic: yes/no questions with the voice or {{آیا}}; question words in the answer's place: {{کجا}}, {{چه}}, {{کی}}, {{چند}}, {{چطور}}, {{چرا}}

goal.t: ببخشید، ایستگاه مترو کجاست؟
goal.r: bebakhshid, istgâh-e metro kojâst?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the metro station?

dialog.tr: Are you a student?
Yes. And you?

dialog.t: من معلم هستم. شما اهل کجا هستید؟
dialog.r: man mo'allem hastam. shomâ ahl-e kojâ hastid?
dialog.tr: I'm a teacher. Where are you from?
I'm from London.
Why Persian?
Because my wife is Iranian!

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions.** Say the sentence and raise your voice at the end: {{شما دانشجو هستید؟|shomâ dâneshju hastid?}} “Are you a student?”. Nothing else changes. In writing, or to sound careful, you can begin with {{آیا|âyâ}}, a word that only says “here comes a question”: {{آیا شما دانشجو هستید؟}}

**Question words stay where the answer goes.** English moves “where” to the front; Persian leaves it in the answer's place. The answer: {{اهل لندن هستم.|ahl-e landan hastam.}} “I'm from London.” The question: {{اهل کجا هستید؟|ahl-e kojâ hastid?}}, “from where are you?”. Put the question word where the answer would be, and you have your question.

table: {{او کیست؟|u kist?}} Who's he? Who's she?
{{کلاس کی است؟|kelâs key ast?}} When's the class?
{{حالت چطور است؟|hâlat chetowr ast?}} How are you?
{{این چند است؟|in chand ast?}} How much is this?
{{چرا خسته‌ای؟|cherâ khaste-i?}} Why are you tired?

blocks.p: {{کی}} is two words written the same way: read **ki** it is “who”, read **key** it is “when”. The reading tells you, and so does the sentence.

**Short forms.** After a question word that ends in a vowel, {{است}} loses its first letter and joins on: {{کجا}} + {{است}} → {{کجاست|kojâst}} “where is”, {{چه}} + {{است}} → {{چیست|chist}} “what is”, {{کی}} + {{است}} → {{کیست|kist}} “who is”.

ex.tr: Excuse me, where's the bank?
What day is it today?
How much is this?
Are you Iranian?
ex.note: {{آیا}} makes it a little more careful; it can be left out

ex.tr: Why are you here?
Which bag is yours?

blocks.tip: To answer: {{بله|bale}} “yes” ({{آره|âre}} with friends) and {{نه|na}} “no”. To start a question to a stranger, say {{ببخشید|bebakhshid}} “excuse me”.

mistakes.why: The question word goes where the answer would go: “you from where are?”.
The thing you're asking about comes first, then {{کجاست}} “where is”, at the end like every verb.

practice.q: Which question asks “When is the class?”

practice.tr: Where are you from?
Excuse me, where's the bank?

practice.q: Someone at a party asks you questions. Choose your replies.

lines.why: “My name”: {{اسمم}} (or {{اسم من}}). {{اسم شما}} is “your name”.
The answer goes where {{کجا}} was: {{اهل لندن هستم}}.

practice.q: Ask a friend: “Why are you tired?”
Your turn: write two questions you'd ask someone you've just met, each with a different question word.

lessons.title: Say what you have
lessons.summary: Say what you have and don't have (a brother, a car, time, thirty years!), with the endings every Persian verb uses.
lessons.topic: {{داشتن}} “to have”: {{دارم}}… {{ندارم}}; the personal endings; leaving out “I” and “you”

goal.t: دو برادر دارم، ولی خواهر ندارم.
goal.r: do barâdar dâram, vali khâhar nadâram.
goal.tr: I have two brothers, but I don't have a sister.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, do you have water?
Yes, we do. Cold or not?
Cold, please. Do you have bread too?
No, I'm afraid we don't have bread.

blocks.p: **Have.** {{دارم|dâram}} “I have”, {{داری|dâri}} “you have”, {{دارد|dârad}} “he, she has”… The verb is at the end, as always: {{یک ماشین دارم.|yek mâshin dâram.}} “I have a car.”

**The endings say who.** Look at the ends: -am, -i, -ad, -im, -id, -and. They are the same on almost every Persian verb, in almost every tense, so learning them once pays off for good. And because the ending already says who, {{من}}, {{تو}}… are usually left out: {{دارم}} alone is “I have”. Say {{من دارم}} only to stress it: “**I** have”.

blocks.means: who or what does the action: “I” in “I have”. In Persian the verb's ending shows it, so the word itself is often left out.

blocks.p: **Not.** Put {{نـ|na-}} on the front of the verb: {{ندارم|nadâram}} “I don't have”. Almost every Persian verb is made negative this way.
**Age.** Persian “has” years: {{بیست سال دارم.|bist sâl dâram.}} “I'm twenty.” And {{چند سال دارید؟|chand sâl dârid?}} “How old are you?”

ex.tr: I have a sister.
Do you have time?
ex.note: to a friend; a question by the voice

ex.tr: She doesn't have a car.
I'm thirty.
ex.note: word for word “I have thirty years”

ex.tr: Do you have a free room?
We don't have children.

blocks.tip: Most Persian verbs have {{می|mi-}} in front in the present ({{می‌خواهم|mi-khâham}} “I want”, next lesson). {{دارم}} is one of the few that don't.

mistakes.why: The verb comes last.
Persian “has” years: {{بیست سال دارم}}.

practice.tr: She has two children.

practice.q: At a small shop. Choose your replies.

lines.why: The verb last, in a question too: {{نان دارید؟}}
“Thanks a lot”: {{خیلی ممنون}}.

practice.tr: I don't have time today.

practice.q: Ask someone politely how old they are.

practice.tr: My brother has a red car.
practice.why: “My brother”: {{برادرم}}, the thing and then its owner.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you have and don't have: family, a car, a pet, time… Use {{دارم}} and {{ندارم}}.

answers.t: یک برادر و یک خواهر دارم.
answers.r: yek barâdar va yek khâhar dâram.
answers.tr: I have a brother and a sister.

answers.t: ماشین ندارم، ولی یک دوچرخه دارم.
answers.r: mâshin nadâram, vali yek docharkhe dâram.
answers.tr: I don't have a car, but I have a bike.

answers.r: yek gorbe dâram. esmash pishi ast.
answers.tr: I have a cat. Her name is Pishi.

lessons.title: Ask for what you want
lessons.summary: Order in a café, ask for things in a shop and say what you'd like, with {{می‌خواهم}} and {{لطفاً}}.
lessons.topic: {{می‌خواهم}} “I want” + a thing; the {{می}} of the present; {{با}} and {{بدون}} “with, without”

goal.t: یک قهوه می‌خواهم، بدون شکر.
goal.r: yek ghahve mi-khâham, bedun-e shekar.
goal.tr: I'd like a coffee, without sugar.

dialog.t: سلام، خوش آمدید! چه میل دارید؟
dialog.r: salâm, khosh âmadid! che meyl dârid?
dialog.tr: Hello, welcome! What would you like?
I'd like a tea, please.
With a pastry?
No, thanks. Just tea.
Certainly.

blocks.p: **I want.** {{می‌خواهم|mi-khâham}} is “I want”, and in a café or a shop “I'd like”. The thing comes first, the verb last: {{یک چای می‌خواهم.|yek chây mi-khâham.}} “I'd like a tea.” Add {{لطفاً|lotfan}} “please”, at the start or at the end.

**The present has {{می}} in front.** {{می‌خواهم}} is three pieces: {{می|mi-}}, which marks the present; {{خواه|khâh}}, the verb itself; and -am, “I”. Almost every Persian verb in the present looks like this, with the endings you met with {{دارم}}. Persian leaves a small gap after {{می}} (the hyphen in the reading). And {{خواه}} has a silent {{و}}: say khâh.
**Not.** {{نـ}} goes in front of {{می}}, and its vowel becomes e: {{نمی‌خواهم|nemi-khâham}} “I don't want”.
**With and without.** {{با|bâ}} “with”, {{بدون|bedun}} “without”, which joins the next word with an ezafe: {{بدون شکر|bedun-e shekar}} “without sugar”.

ex.tr: I'd like a mineral water.
We'd like two tickets, please.
ex.note: after a number the noun stays singular (next lesson)

ex.tr: What do you want?
I don't want coffee, I want tea.
Do you have a sandwich without meat?
He wants a new bike.

blocks.tip: {{چشم|cheshm}}, “eye”, is how a waiter or a shopkeeper says “certainly”: “(on my) eyes”. To call a waiter, say {{ببخشید|bebakhshid}} or {{آقا|âghâ}} “sir”.

mistakes.why: The verb goes last, after the thing you want.
“Not” comes first, before {{می}}: {{نمی‌خواهم}}.

practice.tr: We'd like two coffees.

practice.q: How do you say “I don't want”?
At a café. Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{دارم}} is “I have”; to ask for something, {{می‌خواهم}}.
{{فقط|faghat}} is “only, just”. ({{بدون چای}} would be “without tea”!)

practice.tr: I'd like a coffee without sugar.

practice.q: Your turn: you're in a café. Order two things, and say one thing you don't want. Use {{می‌خواهم}} and {{نمی‌خواهم}}.

answers.t: یک قهوه و یک کیک می‌خواهم، لطفاً. شکر نمی‌خواهم.
answers.r: yek ghahve va yek keyk mi-khâham, lotfan. shekar nemi-khâham.
answers.tr: I'd like a coffee and a cake, please. I don't want sugar.

answers.t: یک چای می‌خواهم، بدون شکر.
answers.r: yek chây mi-khâham, bedun-e shekar.
answers.tr: I'd like a tea, without sugar.

lessons.title: Count, and ask what it costs
lessons.summary: Count to a hundred and beyond, say “two tickets” and “these books”, and ask how much things are.
lessons.topic: numbers; a noun after a number stays singular; plurals with {{ها}} and {{ان}}; {{چند}} and {{چقدر}}

goal.t: دو بلیت می‌خواهم. چقدر می‌شود؟
goal.r: do belit mi-khâham. cheghadr mi-shavad?
goal.tr: I'd like two tickets. How much is that?

dialog.t: ببخشید، این سیب‌ها کیلویی چند است؟
dialog.r: bebakhshid, in sib-hâ kiluyi chand ast?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, how much are these apples a kilo?
Fifty thousand tomans a kilo.

dialog.t: دو کیلو می‌خواهم. پرتقال هم دارید؟
dialog.r: do kilu mi-khâham. porteghâl ham dârid?
dialog.tr: I'd like two kilos. Do you have oranges too?
Yes. The oranges are very good!

dialog.t: سه تا پرتقال، لطفاً. همه چقدر می‌شود؟
dialog.r: se tâ porteghâl, lotfan. hame cheghadr mi-shavad?
dialog.tr: Three oranges, please. How much is it all together?
A hundred and fifty thousand tomans.

blocks.p: **Numbers.** {{یک|yek}} 1, {{دو|do}} 2, {{سه|se}} 3, {{چهار|chahâr}} 4, {{پنج|panj}} 5, {{شش|shesh}} 6, {{هفت|haft}} 7, {{هشت|hasht}} 8, {{نه|noh}} 9, {{ده|dah}} 10; {{یازده|yâzdah}} 11, {{دوازده|davâzdah}} 12; {{بیست|bist}} 20, {{سی|si}} 30, {{چهل|chehel}} 40, {{پنجاه|panjâh}} 50, {{صد|sad}} 100, {{هزار|hezâr}} 1000. Join them with {{و}} “and”, said **o**: {{بیست و پنج|bist o panj}} 25.

blocks.means: the form of a noun that means more than one: books, children.

blocks.p: **After a number, the noun stays singular.** {{دو کتاب|do ketâb}} “two books”, {{سه بلیت|se belit}} “three tickets”: the number already says how many.

**More than one, without a number:** add {{ها|hâ}}, written with a small gap: {{کتاب‌ها|ketâb-hâ}} “(the) books”. Written Persian also uses {{ان|ân}} for people: {{دوستان|dustân}} “friends”, {{دانشجویان|dâneshjuyân}} “students”; in speech {{ها}} works for everything. “This” and “that” don't change: {{این سیب‌ها|in sib-hâ}} “these apples”, word for word “this apples”.

**How much?** {{چند|chand}} is “how much, how many”: {{این چند است؟|in chand ast?}} “How much is this?”. {{چقدر|cheghadr}} “how much” for an amount or a total: {{چقدر می‌شود؟|cheghadr mi-shavad?}} “How much does it come to?”.

ex.tr: They have three children.
These books are mine.
ex.note: things in the plural often take a singular verb

ex.tr: How much is a ticket?
That's a hundred thousand tomans.
My friends are here.
How old are you?
ex.note: to a friend: lesson 6's age, with {{چند}}

blocks.tip: Prices are said in **tomans** (one toman is ten rials, the official unit, and price tags often show rials). The number, then {{تومان|tomân}}, with no plural: {{ده هزار تومان|dah hezâr tomân}} “ten thousand tomans”.
In everyday speech people count things with {{تا|tâ}}: {{سه تا پرتقال|se tâ porteghâl}} “three oranges”, {{چند تا؟|chand tâ?}} “how many?”.

mistakes.why: After a number the noun stays singular: the number already says “more than one”.
Before a noun, {{این}} “this” stays as it is. ({{این‌ها|in-hâ}} on its own means “these ones”.)

practice.tr: I'd like three tickets.

practice.q: At a fruit stall. Choose your replies.

lines.why: After a number, no {{ها}}: {{دو کیلو سیب}}.
{{چقدر می‌شود؟}} is “how much is it?”. ({{چند تا هستید؟}} asks how many people you are!)

practice.tr: These apples are very good.

practice.q: Your turn: in a shop, ask how much something is, and ask for two or three of it. Use {{چند است؟}} and a number.

answers.t: ببخشید، این دفتر چند است؟ سه دفتر می‌خواهم.
answers.r: bebakhshid, in daftar chand ast? se daftar mi-khâham.
answers.tr: Excuse me, how much is this notebook? I'd like three notebooks.

answers.t: این نان‌ها چند است؟ دو تا، لطفاً.
answers.r: in nân-hâ chand ast? do tâ, lotfan.
answers.tr: How much is this bread? Two, please.

lessons.title: Say where things are
lessons.summary: Say “on the table”, “next to the bank” and “in Tehran”, and ask where things are.
lessons.topic: {{در}}, {{به}}, {{از}}; {{روی}}, {{زیر}}, {{کنار}}, {{جلوی}}, {{پشت}}, {{بین}} with the ezafe

goal.t: داروخانه کنار بانک است.
goal.r: dârukhâne kenâr-e bânk ast.
goal.tr: The pharmacy is next to the bank.

dialog.tr: Where are my keys?
Aren't they on the table?
No, they're not on the table.
Are they in your bag?

dialog.t: نه… آهان، اینجاست! زیر کتاب است.
dialog.r: na… âhân, injâst! zir-e ketâb ast.
dialog.tr: No… oh, here they are! Under the book.

blocks.p: **In, to, from.** Three short words do most of the work: {{در|dar}} “in, at”, {{به|be}} “to”, {{از|az}} “from”. As in English, they come **before** the place: {{در تهران|dar tehrân}} “in Tehran”, {{به ایران|be irân}} “to Iran”, {{از لندن|az landan}} “from London”.

blocks.means: a little word before a noun that says where, when or how: in, on, to, from, with.

blocks.p: **On, under, next to: the ezafe again.** Words like “on” and “next to” are really nouns (“top”, “side”), so they join the place with an ezafe: {{روی میز|ru-ye miz}} “on the table” (“top-of table”), {{زیر میز|zir-e miz}} “under the table”, {{کنار بانک|kenâr-e bânk}} “next to the bank”.

table: {{جلوی سینما|jelo-ye sinamâ}} in front of the cinema
{{بین بانک و مسجد|beyn-e bânk va masjed}} between the bank and the mosque

blocks.p: **Where is it?** The thing, the place, then {{است}}: {{داروخانه کنار بانک است.|dârukhâne kenâr-e bânk ast.}} To ask: {{… کجاست؟}} “where is…?”. Things in the plural often take a singular verb: {{کلید‌ها روی میز است.|kelid-hâ ru-ye miz ast.}} “The keys are on the table.”

ex.tr: The book is on the table.
The cat is under the bed.
We're in Tehran.
The bus stop is in front of the university.
My mother isn't at home now.

ex.t: خانهٔ ما بین پارک و مدرسه است.
ex.r: khâne-ye mâ beyn-e pârk va madrese ast.
ex.tr: Our house is between the park and the school.

blocks.tip: {{اینجا|injâ}} “here” and {{آنجا|ânjâ}} “there” need no little word: {{اینجاست|injâst}} “it's here”. In speech you'll also hear {{توی|tu-ye}} for “in”: {{توی کیفم|tu-ye kifam}} “in my bag”.

mistakes.tr: The book is on the table.
mistakes.why: “On” comes before the place, as in English: {{روی میز}}.

mistakes.tr: The book is on the table.
mistakes.why: The thing first, then the place, and {{است}} last.

practice.tr: The pharmacy is next to the bank.
practice.why: “Next to” is {{کنار}}, with the ezafe: kenâr-e bânk.

practice.q: A stranger asks you the way. Choose your replies.

lines.why: “Next to the cinema” is {{کنار سینما}}; {{سینماست}} is {{سینما}} + {{است}}.
The little word first, then the place: {{جلوی پارک}}.

practice.tr: Our house is near here.

practice.q: Say: “My keys are in my bag.”
Your turn: say where things are in your room or your street, with {{روی}}, {{زیر}}, {{کنار}} or {{نزدیک}}.

answers.t: تلفنم روی میز است و کیفم زیر صندلی است.
answers.r: telefonam ru-ye miz ast va kifam zir-e sandali ast.
answers.tr: My phone is on the table and my bag is under the chair.

answers.t: خانهٔ من نزدیک یک پارک است.
answers.r: khâne-ye man nazdik-e yek pârk ast.
answers.tr: My house is near a park.

lessons.title: Say what there is and isn't
lessons.summary: Ask “Is there a pharmacy near here?”, and say what there is, what there isn't, and that there's none at all.
lessons.topic: {{هست}} “there is” and {{نیست}} “there isn't”; {{وجود دارد}}; {{هیچ}} with a negative; the -i of “a”

goal.t: ببخشید، این نزدیکی داروخانه هست؟
goal.r: bebakhshid, in nazdiki dârukhâne hast?
goal.tr: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?

dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there internet in the hotel?

dialog.t: بله، هست. رمزش روی کارت است.
dialog.r: bale, hast. ramzash ru-ye kârt ast.
dialog.tr: Yes, there is. The password is on the card.
Is there a restaurant too?

dialog.t: نه، متأسفانه رستوران نیست، ولی یک کافهٔ خوب کنار هتل هست.
dialog.r: na, mota'assefâne resturân nist, vali yek kâfe-ye khub kenâr-e hotel hast.
dialog.tr: No, I'm afraid there isn't a restaurant, but there's a good café next to the hotel.
Great, thanks!

blocks.p: **There is.** {{هست|hast}}, at the end, says that something is there: {{اینجا یک بانک هست.|injâ yek bânk hast.}} “There's a bank here.” As a question, just with the voice: {{… هست؟}} “Is there…?”. Its “not” is {{نیست|nist}}: {{اینجا بانک نیست.|injâ bânk nist.}} “There's no bank here.”

**{{است}} or {{هست}}?** {{است}} says what or where something is: {{بانک کنار پارک است.|bânk kenâr-e pârk ast.}} “The bank is next to the park.” {{هست}} says that it exists: {{بانک هست.|bânk hast.}} “There is a bank.” Their “not” is the same word, {{نیست}}.

**In writing**, “there is” is often {{وجود دارد|vojud dârad}}, “existence has”: {{در این شهر دو دانشگاه وجود دارد.|dar in shahr do dâneshgâh vojud dârad.}} “There are two universities in this city.” Plural or not, the verb stays {{دارد}}.

**None at all.** {{هیچ|hich}} “no, not any” goes with a negative verb: {{هیچ رستورانی نیست.|hich resturâni nist.}} “There's no restaurant at all.” In Persian two negatives make it stronger; they don't cancel out.

blocks.means: saying “a” or “some”: one of many, not a particular one. In Persian an -i on the end of the noun often does this: {{رستورانی|resturâni}} “a restaurant”.

blocks.p: **The -i of “a”.** A noun can take an ending {{ی}}, said -i, meaning “a, some”: {{کتابی|ketâbi}} “a book”, often together with {{یک}}: {{یک کافه‌ای|yek kâfe-i}} “a café”. You need it after {{هیچ}} ({{هیچ رستورانی}}), and you'll meet it again when you describe which one you mean.

ex.tr: There's a good café here.
Is there any milk in the fridge?
There's no class today.
There's no problem at all.

ex.t: در این خیابان سه رستوران وجود دارد.
ex.r: dar in khiyâbân se resturân vojud dârad.
ex.tr: There are three restaurants on this street.
There's nobody home.

blocks.tip: {{این نزدیکی|in nazdiki}} “near here, around here” (word for word “this nearness”) is the phrase for asking about places: {{این نزدیکی بانک هست؟}}

mistakes.why: To say that something exists, use {{هست}}; {{است}} says what or where something is.
{{هیچ}} needs a negative verb with it: {{نیست}}.

practice.tr: Is there a pharmacy near here?

practice.why: {{هیچ}} with a negative verb: “nobody at all”.

practice.q: At a hotel. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Here you are, this is your room key.

lines.why: To ask whether there is internet: {{هست}}.

lines.t: بله، هست. رمزش روی کارت است.
lines.r: bale, hast. ramzash ru-ye kârt ast.
lines.tr: Yes, there is. The password is on the card.

lines.why: “Is there…?” is {{… هست؟}}, at the end.

lines.t: بله، کنار بانک یک رستوران خوب هست.
lines.r: bale, kenâr-e bânk yek resturân-e khub hast.
lines.tr: Yes, there's a good restaurant next to the bank.

practice.tr: There's no class today.

practice.q: Say: “There's a good café next to the hotel.”
practice.answer: کنار هتل یک کافهٔ خوب هست.
practice.r: kenâr-e hotel yek kâfe-ye khub hast.

practice.q: Your turn: say what there is and isn't in your town or your street. Use {{هست}} and {{نیست}}.

answers.t: در شهر من یک دانشگاه بزرگ هست، ولی فرودگاه نیست.
answers.r: dar shahr-e man yek dâneshgâh-e bozorg hast, vali forudgâh nist.
answers.tr: In my town there's a big university, but there's no airport.

answers.t: در خیابان ما دو کافه هست.
answers.r: dar khiyâbân-e mâ do kâfe hast.
answers.tr: There are two cafés on our street.

lessons.title: Say where you're going, and how
lessons.summary: Say where you're going and where you're coming from, by bus, by taxi or on foot: your first everyday verbs in the present.
lessons.topic: the present of {{رفتن}} “go” and {{آمدن}} “come”: {{می‌روم}}, {{می‌آیم}}; the present stem; {{به}} + a place, {{با}} + transport

goal.t: فردا با اتوبوس به اصفهان می‌روم.
goal.r: fardâ bâ otobus be esfahân mi-ravam.
goal.tr: Tomorrow I'm going to Isfahan by bus.

dialog.tr: Hi! Where are you going?

dialog.t: به دانشگاه می‌روم. تو هم می‌آیی؟
dialog.r: be dâneshgâh mi-ravam. to ham mi-âyi?
dialog.tr: I'm going to the university. Are you coming too?

dialog.t: نه، به خانه می‌روم. با مترو می‌روی؟
dialog.r: na, be khâne mi-ravam. bâ metro mi-ravi?
dialog.tr: No, I'm going home. Are you going by metro?
No, I'm walking. It's close.
OK, see you tomorrow!

blocks.p: **Go and come.** {{می‌روم|mi-ravam}} is “I go” and “I'm going”, {{می‌آیم|mi-âyam}} “I come” and “I'm coming”. Persian has one present tense for both: {{به دانشگاه می‌روم.}} is “I go to the university” and “I'm going to the university”.

**Where to:** {{به|be}} + the place: {{به ایران|be irân}} “to Iran”. **Where from:** {{از|az}}: {{از سر کار می‌آیم.|az sar-e kâr mi-âyam.}} “I'm coming from work.” **How:** {{با|bâ}} + the transport: {{با تاکسی|bâ tâksi}} “by taxi”, {{با قطار|bâ ghatâr}} “by train”; on foot is {{پیاده|piyâde}}. The verb comes last, as always; a common order is when, how, where, verb: {{فردا با اتوبوس به اصفهان می‌روم.}}

blocks.means: the main part of a verb, which the other pieces are added to: in {{می‌روم|mi-ravam}} “I go”, the stem is {{رو|rav}}.

blocks.p: **The present stem.** A Persian verb in the present is {{می}} + its present **stem** + the ending. The stem of “go” is {{رو|rav}}; the stem of “come” is {{آ|â}}, with a y before the ending ({{می‌آیم|mi-âyam}}). These stems don't look much like the dictionary forms, {{رفتن|raftan}} “to go” and {{آمدن|âmadan}} “to come”, so learn each verb with its stem: the next lesson shows how.

ex.t: هر روز با مترو سر کار می‌روم.
ex.r: har ruz bâ metro sar-e kâr mi-ravam.
ex.tr: I go to work by metro every day.
When are you coming?
He's coming from Shiraz.
We're going to the cinema tonight.

ex.t: با تاکسی می‌روید یا با اتوبوس؟
ex.r: bâ tâksi mi-ravid yâ bâ otobus?
ex.tr: Are you going by taxi or by bus?
I'm not going home.

blocks.tip: In everyday speech these verbs shrink: {{می‌روم}} is said {{می‌رم|miram}}, {{می‌روی}} {{می‌ری|miri}}. You'll hear them all the time; learn the full forms first, the short ones come by themselves.

mistakes.why: The verb goes last, after the place.
{{پیاده}} “on foot” needs no {{با}}: {{با}} is for what you ride in.

practice.tr: We're going to Tehran tomorrow.

practice.q: A friend meets you in the street. Choose your replies.

options: به خانه می‌روی. خیلی خسته است!
lines.why: About yourself: {{می‌روم}} and {{خسته‌ام}}.
rs: be khâne mi-ravi. kheyli khaste ast!

lines.why: By bus: {{با اتوبوس}}. ({{به اتوبوس}} would be “to the bus”.)

practice.tr: I go to work by metro every day.

practice.q: Ask a friend: “When are you coming?”
Your turn: say where you're going this week, and how. Use {{به … می‌روم}} and {{با}}.

answers.t: فردا با قطار به مشهد می‌روم.
answers.r: fardâ bâ ghatâr be mashhad mi-ravam.
answers.tr: Tomorrow I'm going to Mashhad by train.

answers.t: امشب با دوستانم به رستوران می‌رویم.
answers.r: emshab bâ dustânam be resturân mi-ravim.
answers.tr: Tonight my friends and I are going to a restaurant.

answers.t: هر روز پیاده سر کار می‌روم.
answers.r: har ruz piyâde sar-e kâr mi-ravam.
answers.tr: I walk to work every day.

lessons.title: Say what you do every day
lessons.summary: Talk about your day (get up, eat, read, sleep) with any verb in the present, and meet the two stems every Persian verb has.
lessons.topic: the present tense of any verb; the two stems: past stem ({{خورد}}) and present stem ({{خور}}); time words

goal.t: صبح‌ها چای می‌خورم و روزنامه می‌خوانم.
goal.r: sobh-hâ chây mi-khoram va ruznâme mi-khânam.
goal.tr: In the mornings I drink tea and read the paper.

dialog.tr: What do you do in the mornings?

dialog.t: ساعت هفت بیدار می‌شوم، صبحانه می‌خورم و به دانشگاه می‌روم.
dialog.r: sâ'at-e haft bidâr mi-shavam, sobhâne mi-khoram va be dâneshgâh mi-ravam.
dialog.tr: I get up at seven, have breakfast and go to the university.
What do you have for breakfast?

dialog.t: نان و پنیر و چای. تو چطور؟
dialog.r: nân o panir o chây. to chetowr?
dialog.tr: Bread, cheese and tea. What about you?

dialog.t: من صبحانه نمی‌خورم. فقط قهوه می‌خورم!
dialog.r: man sobhâne nemi-khoram. faghat ghahve mi-khoram!
dialog.tr: I don't eat breakfast. I just have coffee!

blocks.p: **Every verb, one pattern.** In the present, a Persian verb is {{می}} + its present stem + the ending you know: {{می‌خورم|mi-khoram}} “I eat”, {{می‌خوانی|mi-khâni}} “you read”, {{می‌نویسد|mi-nevisad}} “she writes”. As with {{می‌روم}}, it means both “I eat” and “I'm eating”.

blocks.means: the dictionary form of a verb, “to …”: {{خوردن|khordan}} “to eat”. In Persian it ends in -an.

blocks.p: **Two stems.** Every Persian verb has two stems. The **past stem** is the infinitive without its -an: {{خوردن}} → {{خورد|khord}}; you'll need it for the past. The **present stem** is the one for now, and you learn it with the verb, because it can look quite different: {{خوردن}} → {{خور|khor}}, but {{دیدن|didan}} “to see” → {{بین|bin}}. So learn each new verb as a set of three: {{خوردن}}, {{خورد}}, {{خور}}.

**Good news:** verbs in -idan, like {{خوابیدن}} and {{خریدن}}, are regular: drop the -idan and you have the present stem ({{خواب}}, {{خر}}). The irregular ones are few, and so common that you'll learn them fast.

**When.** Time words usually come early, before the place and the verb: {{هر روز|har ruz}} “every day”, {{صبح‌ها|sobh-hâ}} “in the mornings”, {{شب‌ها|shab-hâ}} “in the evenings, at night”, {{بعد از ظهر|ba'd az zohr}} “in the afternoon”.

ex.tr: I read in the evenings.
My father watches the news every night.
I usually go to bed at eleven.
Do you buy bread from this shop?
The children are playing in the park.
What do you eat in the mornings?

blocks.tip: {{خوردن}} is “eat”, and in everyday Persian also “drink”: {{چای می‌خورم.|chây mi-khoram.}} “I drink tea.”

mistakes.why: The verb goes last.

mistakes.tr: I watch a film every night.
mistakes.why: The present is made with the present stem, {{بین}}, not the past stem {{دید}}. ({{می‌دیدم}} is a past form, “I used to watch”, for later.)

practice.tr: I drink tea every morning.

practice.q: The present stem of {{دیدن}} “to see” is…
practice.why: {{دیدن}} is irregular: its present stem is {{بین|bin}}, as in {{می‌بینم}} “I see”.

practice.tr: She reads at night.
In the mornings I drink tea and read the paper.

practice.q: A new friend asks about your day. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What do you do in the mornings?

options: صبحانه می‌خورم و سر کار می‌روم.
صبحانه می‌خورد و سر کار می‌رود.
lines.why: About yourself, -am: {{می‌خورم}}, {{می‌روم}}.
rs: sobhâne mi-khoram va sar-e kâr mi-ravam.
sobhâne mi-khorad va sar-e kâr mi-ravad.

lines.why: {{با مترو}} goes before the verb, which comes last.

practice.q: Say: “I usually go to bed at eleven.”
Your turn: describe your morning in two or three sentences, with verbs in the present.

answers.t: ساعت هشت بیدار می‌شوم. صبحانه نمی‌خورم، فقط قهوه می‌خورم.
answers.r: sâ'at-e hasht bidâr mi-shavam. sobhâne nemi-khoram, faghat ghahve mi-khoram.
answers.tr: I wake up at eight. I don't eat breakfast, I just have coffee.

answers.t: صبح‌ها روزنامه می‌خوانم و با اتوبوس سر کار می‌روم.
answers.r: sobh-hâ ruznâme mi-khânam va bâ otobus sar-e kâr mi-ravam.
answers.tr: In the mornings I read the paper and go to work by bus.

lessons.title: Say what you don't do, and how often
lessons.summary: Say “I never eat meat”, “I sometimes go to the cinema” and “I don't smoke”.
lessons.topic: {{نمی}} + verb; {{همیشه}}, {{معمولاً}}, {{گاهی}}; {{هیچ‌وقت}} and {{اصلاً}} with a negative verb

goal.t: من هیچ‌وقت گوشت نمی‌خورم.
goal.r: man hich-vaght gusht nemi-khoram.
goal.tr: I never eat meat.

dialog.tr: Will you have some kebab?
I'm sorry, I don't eat meat.
Not at all? Don't you eat fish either?

dialog.t: گاهی ماهی می‌خورم، ولی گوشت هیچ‌وقت.
dialog.r: gâhi mâhi mi-khoram, vali gusht hich-vaght.
dialog.tr: I sometimes eat fish, but meat never.
Then do have some rice and herbs!

blocks.p: **Not.** Put {{نمی|nemi-}} in the place of {{می}}: {{می‌خورم}} “I eat” → {{نمی‌خورم|nemi-khoram}} “I don't eat”. The stem and the ending don't change.
**How often.** These words come early in the sentence, usually after the subject: {{همیشه|hamishe}} “always”, {{معمولاً|ma'mulan}} “usually”, {{اغلب|aghlab}} “often”, {{گاهی|gâhi}} “sometimes”.

**Never.** {{هیچ‌وقت|hich-vaght}} “never” (word for word “no time”) needs a negative verb with it, just like {{هیچ}} in lesson 10: {{هیچ‌وقت دیر نمی‌آید.|hich-vaght dir nemi-âyad.}} “She's never late.” And {{اصلاً|aslan}} with a negative verb is “not at all”: {{اصلاً نمی‌دانم.|aslan nemi-dânam.}} “I have no idea.”

table: {{همیشه چای می‌خورم.|hamishe chây mi-khoram.}} I always drink tea.
{{معمولاً پیاده می‌روم.|ma'mulan piyâde mi-ravam.}} I usually walk.
{{گاهی به سینما می‌رویم.|gâhi be sinamâ mi-ravim.}} We sometimes go to the cinema.
{{هیچ‌وقت تلویزیون نمی‌بینم.|hich-vaght televiziyon nemi-binam.}} I never watch TV.
{{اصلاً قهوه نمی‌خورد.|aslan ghahve nemi-khorad.}} He doesn't drink coffee at all.

ex.tr: I don't smoke.
He usually doesn't work at night.

ex.t: ما همیشه جمعه‌ها به پارک می‌رویم.
ex.r: mâ hamishe jom'e-hâ be pârk mi-ravim.
ex.tr: We always go to the park on Fridays.
ex.note: Friday is the weekend in Iran

ex.tr: She's never late.
ex.note: word for word “she never comes late”

ex.tr: I have no idea.

ex.t: گاهی با دوستانم فوتبال بازی می‌کنم.
ex.r: gâhi bâ dustânam futbâl bâzi mi-konam.
ex.tr: Sometimes I play football with my friends.

blocks.tip: {{نمی‌دانم|nemi-dânam}} “I don't know” is one of the most useful sentences there is. In speech it shrinks to {{نمی‌دونم|nemi-dunam}}.

mistakes.why: {{هیچ‌وقت}} “never” needs a negative verb: {{نمی‌خورم}}.
“Not” is part of the verb: {{نمی}} in the place of {{می}}. {{نه}} on its own is “no”.

practice.tr: I don't drink coffee.

practice.q: Dinner with a friend's family. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Will you have tea or coffee?

lines.why: {{نمی‌خورم}}: ne-mi-khoram.
“Never” is {{هیچ‌وقت}} with a negative verb. ({{همیشه … نمی‌خورم}} sounds like “I always don't”.)

practice.tr: We always go to the park on Fridays.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you never do and one thing you sometimes do. Use {{هیچ‌وقت … نمی}} and {{گاهی}}.

answers.t: هیچ‌وقت سیگار نمی‌کشم. گاهی به سینما می‌روم.
answers.r: hich-vaght sigâr nemi-kesham. gâhi be sinamâ mi-ravam.
answers.tr: I never smoke. Sometimes I go to the cinema.

answers.t: هیچ‌وقت صبحانه نمی‌خورم و هیچ‌وقت زود نمی‌خوابم.
answers.r: hich-vaght sobhâne nemi-khoram va hich-vaght zud nemi-khâbam.
answers.tr: I never eat breakfast and I never go to bed early.

lessons.title: Talk about work, study and calls
lessons.summary: Say “I work”, “I'm studying”, “I'll call you” and “I'm listening”: most everyday Persian actions are a noun plus “do”, “hit” or “give”.
lessons.topic: compound verbs: {{کار کردن}}, {{درس خواندن}}, {{زنگ زدن}}, {{صحبت کردن}}, {{گوش دادن}}; where {{نمی}} goes

goal.t: در یک بانک کار می‌کنم و شب‌ها فارسی یاد می‌گیرم.
goal.r: dar yek bânk kâr mi-konam va shab-hâ fârsi yâd mi-giram.
goal.tr: I work in a bank, and in the evenings I learn Persian.

dialog.t: الو؟ سلام عزیزم! چه کار می‌کنی؟
dialog.r: alo? salâm azizam! che kâr mi-koni?
dialog.tr: Hello? Hi, sweetheart! What are you doing?

dialog.t: سلام مامان! درس می‌خوانم. فردا امتحان دارم.
dialog.r: salâm mâmân! dars mi-khânam. fardâ emtehân dâram.
dialog.tr: Hi, Mum! I'm studying. I have an exam tomorrow.
OK, then I'll call later.

dialog.t: نه، الان وقت دارم. گوش می‌کنم!
dialog.r: na, al'ân vaght dâram. gush mi-konam!
dialog.tr: No, I have time now. I'm listening!

blocks.p: **Noun + verb.** Persian has fewer simple verbs than English. Most everyday actions are a noun or an adjective plus a common verb: {{کار|kâr}} “work” + {{کردن|kardan}} “do” = {{کار کردن}} “to work”; {{زنگ|zang}} “bell” + {{زدن|zadan}} “hit” = {{زنگ زدن}} “to ring, to call”.

blocks.means: a verb made of two words, a noun (or an adjective) and a common verb, which together mean one action: {{کار کردن|kâr kardan}} “to work”.

blocks.p: **Only the verb part changes.** The first word stays as it is; {{می}}, the stem and the ending go on the verb: {{کار می‌کنم|kâr mi-konam}} “I work”, {{زنگ می‌زنی|zang mi-zani}} “you call”. “Not” goes on the verb part too: {{کار نمی‌کنم|kâr nemi-konam}} “I don't work”.

**Four verbs do most of the work:** {{کردن}} “do” (present stem {{کن|kon}}), {{زدن}} “hit” ({{زن|zan}}), {{دادن}} “give” ({{ده|dah}}) and {{گرفتن}} “take” ({{گیر|gir}}). Learn their stems once, and hundreds of verbs are yours.

**Who to?** The person you talk to or call takes {{با}} or {{به}}: {{با او صحبت می‌کنم.|bâ u sohbat mi-konam.}} “I'm talking to him.” {{به مادرم زنگ می‌زنم.|be mâdaram zang mi-zanam.}} “I'm calling my mother.” {{به موسیقی گوش می‌دهم.|be musighi gush mi-daham.}} “I listen to music.”

ex.tr: Where do you work?
She doesn't speak Persian.

ex.t: هر شب به مادرم زنگ می‌زنم.
ex.r: har shab be mâdaram zang mi-zanam.
ex.tr: I call my mother every night.

ex.t: در ماشین به موسیقی گوش می‌دهیم.
ex.r: dar mâshin be musighi gush mi-dahim.
ex.tr: We listen to music in the car.
The children are playing football.
I'll help you.
ex.note: the present is also used for the near future

blocks.tip: New words come into Persian this way too: {{چک کردن|chek kardan}} “to check”, {{پارک کردن|pârk kardan}} “to park”. When you don't know a verb, a noun with {{کردن}} is often what Iranians say.

mistakes.why: {{نمی}} goes on the verb part, {{کنم}}, not on the noun.
{{کار}} is the noun “work”; the verb is {{کار کردن}}: {{کار می‌کنم}}.

practice.tr: I work in a hospital.

practice.t: او هر روز به من زنگ ___.
practice.tr: He calls me every day.
practice.r: u har ruz be man zang ___.

practice.q: How do you say “I don't speak Persian”?
A friend phones you. Choose your replies.

lines.why: “Study” is {{درس خواندن}}, “read lessons”.
{{نمی}} goes on {{کنم}}: {{بازی نمی‌کنم}}.

practice.tr: I call my mother every night.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you do for work or study, and two other things you do every week. Use compound verbs ({{کار می‌کنم}}, {{زنگ می‌زنم}}…).

answers.t: در یک مدرسه کار می‌کنم. هفته‌ای دو بار فوتبال بازی می‌کنم.
answers.r: dar yek madrese kâr mi-konam. hafte-i do bâr futbâl bâzi mi-konam.
answers.tr: I work in a school. I play football twice a week.

answers.t: در دانشگاه درس می‌خوانم و جمعه‌ها به پدر و مادرم زنگ می‌زنم.
answers.r: dar dâneshgâh dars mi-khânam va jom'e-hâ be pedar o mâdaram zang mi-zanam.
answers.tr: I study at university, and on Fridays I call my parents.

lessons.title: Say which thing you mean
lessons.summary: Say “I'd like that red bag” and “I can't find my key”: the little word {{را}} marks the particular thing an action is done to.
lessons.topic: the object; {{را}} after a definite object; {{مرا}}; no {{را}} for “a, any”

goal.t: آن کیف قرمز را می‌خواهم.
goal.r: ân kif-e ghermez râ mi-khâham.
goal.tr: I'd like that red bag.

dialog.tr: Which one would you like?
I'd like that red bag.
This one?

dialog.t: نه، آن یکی را. کنار کیف سیاه.
dialog.r: na, ân yeki râ. kenâr-e kif-e siyâh.
dialog.tr: No, that one. Next to the black bag.
Here you are.

blocks.means: the person or thing an action is done to: “the book” in “I'm reading the book”.

blocks.p: **{{را}}: the one you mean.** When the object is a particular one, one that you and the listener both know, put {{را|râ}} after it: {{کتاب را می‌خوانم.|ketâb râ mi-khânam.}} “I'm reading the book” (the one we were talking about). Without {{را}}: {{کتاب می‌خوانم.|ketâb mi-khânam.}} “I'm reading a book” or “I read books”. So {{را}} does part of the work of English “the”.

**When you need it:** after {{این}} and {{آن}} ({{این فیلم را می‌بینم|in film râ mi-binam}} “I'm watching this film”), after a name ({{سارا را می‌بینم|sârâ râ mi-binam}} “I can see Sara”), after “my, your” ({{کیفم را می‌خواهم|kifam râ mi-khâham}} “I want my bag”), and after a pronoun. It comes after the whole phrase, adjectives and owner included: {{کیف قرمز سارا را|kif-e ghermez-e sârâ râ}} “Sara's red bag”.

**Me, you, him.** {{من}} + {{را}} is usually written as one word, {{مرا|marâ}}; the others are just {{تو را|to râ}}, {{او را|u râ}}, {{ما را|mâ râ}}…: {{او را می‌شناسم.|u râ mi-shenâsam.}} “I know him (her).”
**Not for “to”.** {{را}} is only for the object. The person you talk to or call takes {{با}} or {{به}}, as in the last lesson: {{به سارا زنگ می‌زنم.|be sârâ zang mi-zanam.}} “I'm calling Sara.”

ex.tr: Do you know this film?
ex.note: {{شناختن|shenâkhtan}} “to know (a person, a thing)”, present stem {{شناس|shenâs}}

ex.tr: I read a newspaper every day.
I'm reading today's paper.
I can't see my key.
Do you know Ali?
Forgive me.

blocks.tip: In speech, {{را}} is said {{رو|ro}} after a vowel and just -o after a consonant: {{کتابو|ketâbo}} “the book”. Write {{را}}.

mistakes.why: “This book” is a particular one, so it needs {{را}}.
{{را}} comes after the whole phrase, adjective included: {{کیف قرمز را}}.

options: نه، آن یکی را، کنار کیف قرمز.
نه، آن یکی، کنار قرمز کیف.
lines.why: {{آن یکی|ân yeki}} “that one”, and the adjective after the noun: {{کیف قرمز}}.
rs: na, ân yeki râ, kenâr-e kif-e ghermez.
na, ân yeki, kenâr-e ghermez kif.

practice.tr: I can't see my key.
I'm calling my mother.
practice.why: With {{زنگ زدن}}, the person you call takes {{به}}, not {{را}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say which things around you you'd like, or can't find, with {{را}}.

answers.r: ân ketâb-e âbi râ mi-khâham.
answers.tr: I'd like that blue book.

answers.r: gushi-am râ nemi-binam. kojâst?

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Say what you like and love, what you don't like, and ask others: “Do you like Persian food?”
lessons.topic: {{دوست داشتن}} (with {{را}}); {{از … خوشم می‌آید}}; {{به … علاقه دارم}}

goal.t: غذای ایرانی را خیلی دوست دارم.
goal.r: ghazâ-ye irâni râ kheyli dust dâram.
goal.tr: I really like Persian food.

dialog.tr: Do you like Iranian films?

dialog.t: بله، خیلی! فیلم‌های کیارستمی را خیلی دوست دارم.
dialog.r: bale, kheyli! film-hâ-ye kiyârostami râ kheyli dust dâram.
dialog.tr: Yes, a lot! I love Kiarostami's films.
What about Iranian music?

dialog.t: از موسیقی سنتی خوشم می‌آید، ولی پاپ را دوست ندارم.
dialog.r: az musighi-ye sonnati khosham mi-âyad, vali pâp râ dust nadâram.
dialog.tr: I like traditional music, but I don't like pop.
Me too!

blocks.p: **Like and love.** {{دوست داشتن|dust dâshtan}}, word for word “to have as a friend”, is both “to like” and “to love”. It is a compound verb with {{داشتن}}, so like {{دارم}} it has no {{می}}: {{دوست دارم|dust dâram}} “I like”, {{دوست ندارم|dust nadâram}} “I don't like”. {{خیلی|kheyli}} “very” makes it “really like, love”.

**What you like** comes before it, with {{را}} when it is a particular thing, or a whole kind of thing: {{این آهنگ را دوست دارم.|in âhang râ dust dâram.}} “I like this song.” {{غذای ایرانی را دوست دارم.}} “I like Persian food.” For things in general you may leave {{را}} out: {{چای دوست دارم.|chây dust dâram.}} “I like tea.” People always take {{را}}: {{تو را دوست دارم.|to râ dust dâram.}} “I love you.”

**{{خوشم می‌آید}}.** Another very common way, word for word “my pleasure comes from…”: {{از این شهر خوشم می‌آید.|az in shahr khosham mi-âyad.}} “I like this city.” The thing takes {{از}}, and the person is a possessive ending on {{خوش}}: {{خوشم|khosham}} “I”, {{خوشت|khoshat}} “you”, {{خوشش|khoshash}} “he, she”.

table: {{… را دوست دارم.|… râ dust dâram.}}
{{… را دوست ندارم.|… râ dust nadâram.}}

blocks.p: **Interested in.** {{به … علاقه دارم|be … alâghe dâram}} “I'm interested in…” is for hobbies and subjects: {{به تاریخ علاقه دارم.|be târikh alâghe dâram.}} “I'm interested in history.”

ex.t: من چای و قهوه دوست دارم.
ex.r: man chây va ghahve dust dâram.
ex.tr: I like tea and coffee.

ex.t: این آهنگ را خیلی دوست دارم!
ex.r: in âhang râ kheyli dust dâram!
ex.tr: I love this song!
My brother doesn't like football.
Do you like this restaurant?
I'm interested in Persian poetry.
I love you.

blocks.tip: {{دوست|dust}} on its own is “friend”: {{دوستم|dustam}} is “my friend”, and {{دوست دارم}} “I like”. Iranians love the poet Hafez: {{شعر حافظ را دوست دارید؟|she'r-e hâfez râ dust dârid?}} “Do you like Hafez's poetry?” can start a long conversation.

mistakes.why: Like {{دارم}}, {{دوست دارم}} has no {{می}}.
With {{خوشم می‌آید}}, the thing you like takes {{از}} “from”.

practice.tr: I really like Iranian films.
I like this food.

options: he or she doesn't like it

practice.q: Your Iranian friend's mother asks you questions. Choose your replies.

lines.why: “Like” is {{دوست دارم}}.

options: بله! قورمه‌سبزی را خیلی دوست دارم.
lines.why: {{را}} comes right after the thing: {{قورمه‌سبزی را}}.
rs: bale! ghorme-sabzi râ kheyli dust dâram.

practice.tr: My brother doesn't like football.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you like and one you don't. Try both {{دوست دارم}} and {{از … خوشم می‌آید}}.

answers.r: musighi râ kheyli dust dâram, vali az varzesh khosham nemi-âyad.
answers.tr: I love music, but I don't like sport.

answers.t: از تهران خوشم می‌آید. چای ایرانی را هم دوست دارم.
answers.r: az tehrân khosham mi-âyad. chây-e irâni râ ham dust dâram.

lessons.title: Say when: times and days
lessons.summary: Ask and tell the time, name the days of the week, and say when things happen: “at eight”, “on Saturday”, “the second floor”.
lessons.topic: {{ساعت چند است؟}}; {{ساعت}} + a number; the days of the week; {{صبح}}, {{ظهر}}, {{شب}}; ordinal numbers ({{اول}}, {{دوم}}…)

goal.t: کلاس فارسی شنبه‌ها ساعت شش است.
goal.r: kelâs-e fârsi shanbe-hâ sâ'at-e shesh ast.
goal.tr: The Persian class is on Saturdays at six.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, what time is it?
It's half past five.
Oh no! My class is at six.
Which days is the class?
Saturdays and Mondays.

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{ساعت چند است؟|sâ'at chand ast?}}, word for word “the hour is how many?”. The answer: {{ساعت هفت است.|sâ'at haft ast.}} “It's seven.” “Half” is {{نیم|nim}}, “a quarter” {{ربع|rob'}}: {{هفت و نیم|haft o nim}} “half past seven”, {{هفت و ربع|haft o rob'}} “a quarter past seven”, {{یک ربع به هشت|yek rob' be hasht}} “a quarter to eight”.

**At what time?** {{ساعت}} + the ezafe + the number, with no little word for “at”: {{ساعت هشت سر کار می‌روم.|sâ'at-e hasht sar-e kâr mi-ravam.}} “I go to work at eight.” To ask: {{ساعت چند؟|sâ'at-e chand?}} “At what time?”.

table: the first day of the week
the day of gathering: the weekend

blocks.p: **On Saturday, in the morning.** Days need no little word: {{شنبه می‌آیم.|shanbe mi-âyam.}} “I'm coming on Saturday.” With {{ها}} they mean “every”: {{شنبه‌ها|shanbe-hâ}} “on Saturdays”, {{صبح‌ها|sobh-hâ}} “in the mornings”. The parts of the day: {{صبح|sobh}} “morning”, {{ظهر|zohr}} “noon”, {{بعد از ظهر|ba'd az zohr}} “afternoon”, {{عصر|asr}} “late afternoon”, {{شب|shab}} “evening, night”; and {{امروز|emruz}} “today”, {{فردا|fardâ}} “tomorrow”, {{امشب|emshab}} “tonight”.

**First, second.** Add {{م}}, said -om, to the number: {{دوم|dovvom}} “second”, {{سوم|sevvom}} “third”, {{چهارم|chahârom}} “fourth”; “first” is {{اول|avval}}. They go after the noun, with an ezafe: {{طبقهٔ دوم|tabaghe-ye dovvom}} “the second floor”. With {{ین}} added they go before it: {{اولین بار|avvalin bâr}} “the first time”.

ex.t: ساعت چند است؟ ساعت ده و ربع است.
ex.r: sâ'at chand ast? sâ'at dah o rob' ast.
ex.tr: What time is it? It's a quarter past ten.
The film starts at eight.
I don't work on Fridays.
My office is on the third floor.

ex.t: این اولین بار است که به ایران می‌آیم.
ex.r: in avvalin bâr ast ke be irân mi-âyam.
ex.tr: This is the first time I've come to Iran.
I'll call tonight at nine.

blocks.tip: Iran's week starts on Saturday, and the weekend is Friday (for many, Thursday afternoon too). Iran also has its own calendar, whose year starts at Nowruz, on the first day of spring.

mistakes.why: “At” a time needs no little word: just {{ساعت هشت}}.
{{دو طبقه}} is “two floors”. “Second” is {{دوم}}, after the noun with an ezafe.

practice.tr: The class is at eight.

practice.why: The week starts with {{شنبه}}, Saturday; then {{یک‌شنبه}}, “one-Saturday”, Sunday.

practice.q: Making a plan with a friend. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Are you coming to the cinema tomorrow?

lines.why: “At what time” is {{ساعت چند}}. ({{چند ساعت}} is “how many hours”.)

options: خوب است. در هفت ساعت می‌آیم.
lines.why: “At seven” is just {{ساعت هفت}}. ({{در هفت ساعت}} would be “in seven hours”.)
rs: khub ast. dar haft sâ'at mi-âyam.

practice.tr: I don't work on Fridays.

Your turn: describe your week: what you do on two different days, and at what time.

answers.t: شنبه‌ها ساعت هشت سر کار می‌روم. جمعه‌ها تا ساعت ده می‌خوابم.
answers.r: shanbe-hâ sâ'at-e hasht sar-e kâr mi-ravam. jom'e-hâ tâ sâ'at-e dah mi-khâbam.
answers.tr: On Saturdays I go to work at eight. On Fridays I sleep until ten.

answers.r: doshanbe-hâ sâ'at-e shesh kelâs-e fârsi dâram.

lessons.title: Say how you feel
lessons.summary: Say you're hungry, cold, sleepy or happy, and ask someone how they feel: some of the most Persian sentences there are.
lessons.topic: the short “am, are” again ({{گرسنه‌ام}}); {{سردم است}}, {{خوابم می‌آید}}: feelings with a possessive ending; {{حالم خوب است}}

goal.t: سردم است. پنجره را می‌بندی؟
goal.r: sardam ast. panjere râ mi-bandi?
goal.tr: I'm cold. Will you close the window?

dialog.tr: Are you OK? Are you tired?

dialog.t: نه، خسته نیستم، ولی خیلی گرسنه‌ام!
dialog.r: na, khaste nistam, vali kheyli gorosne-am!
dialog.tr: No, I'm not tired, but I'm really hungry!
Me too. Aren't you cold?
Yes, I'm a bit cold.
Then let's find a restaurant!

blocks.p: **I'm hungry, I'm tired.** Many feelings are adjectives with the short “am, are” of lesson 3: {{گرسنه‌ام|gorosne-am}} “I'm hungry”, {{تشنه‌ام|teshne-am}} “I'm thirsty”, {{خسته‌ام|khaste-am}} “I'm tired”, {{خوشحالم|khoshhâlam}} “I'm happy”, {{ناراحتم|nârâhatam}} “I'm upset”. For “not”: {{نیستم|nistam}}, {{خسته نیستم.|khaste nistam.}}

**I'm cold: “my cold is”.** For some feelings Persian says, word for word, “my cold is”, “my sleep comes”. The person is a possessive ending (lesson 4), and the verb is always the “it” form: {{سردم است.|sardam ast.}} “I'm cold.” {{گرمت است؟|garmat ast?}} “Are you hot?” {{خوابم می‌آید.|khâbam mi-âyad.}} “I'm sleepy.”

**How are you?** {{حالت چطور است؟|hâlat chetowr ast?}}, “how is your state?” (politely {{حالتان|hâletân}}), works the same way: {{حالم خوب است.|hâlam khub ast.}} “I'm well.” {{حالش خوب نیست.|hâlash khub nist.}} “He isn't well.”

ex.tr: I'm really thirsty. Do you have any water?
I'm very happy today!
Are you cold?
The children are sleepy.
My mother is a bit upset.
I don't feel well.

blocks.tip: {{چرا|cherâ}}, “why”, is also the “yes” that answers a negative question: “{{سردت نیست؟}}” “Aren't you cold?”, “{{چرا!}}” “Yes, I am!”. {{بله}} there would be unclear.

mistakes.why: {{من سرد هستم}} says “I am a cold person”. For feeling cold, “my cold is”: {{سردم است}}.
The verb is about “my sleep”, so it stays “it comes”, {{می‌آید}}. The {{م}} on {{خواب}} says who.

practice.tr: Will you close the window? I'm cold.
I'm very hungry. I'd like a sandwich.

practice.q: Your friend looks worried about you. Choose your replies.

options: نه، حالم خوب نیست. خیلی خسته‌ام.
نه، حالت خوب نیست. خیلی خسته‌ای.
lines.why: About yourself: {{حالم}} “my state” and {{خسته‌ام}}.
rs: na, hâlam khub nist. kheyli khaste-am.
na, hâlat khub nist. kheyli khaste-i.

lines.why: {{چرا}} is the yes to a negative question, and “I'm cold” is {{سردم است}}.

practice.tr: The children are sleepy.

practice.q: Your turn: how do you feel right now? Say two things: one with {{…م}}, one with {{…م است}} or {{…م می‌آید}}.

answers.t: کمی خسته‌ام و خوابم می‌آید.
answers.r: kami khaste-am va khâbam mi-âyad.
answers.tr: I'm a bit tired and sleepy.

answers.t: حالم خوب است، ولی گرسنه‌ام!
answers.r: hâlam khub ast, vali gorosne-am!
answers.tr: I'm fine, but I'm hungry!

lessons.title: Say what you want to do
lessons.summary: Say “I want to go to Shiraz”, “I want to learn Persian” and “Do you want to come?”: the subjunctive, the most useful form in Persian.
lessons.topic: the subjunctive: {{بـ}} + present stem + ending ({{بروم}}); {{می‌خواهم}} + subjunctive; compound verbs usually without {{بـ}}

goal.t: می‌خواهم فارسی یاد بگیرم.
goal.r: mi-khâham fârsi yâd begiram.
goal.tr: I want to learn Persian.

dialog.tr: Where do you want to go in the summer?

dialog.t: می‌خواهم به شیراز بروم. می‌خواهم حافظیه را ببینم.
dialog.r: mi-khâham be shirâz beravam. mi-khâham hâfeziye râ bebinam.
dialog.tr: I want to go to Shiraz. I want to see the tomb of Hafez.
I want to come too!
Great! We'll go together.

blocks.p: **Two verbs, both with an ending.** In {{می‌خواهم بروم|mi-khâham beravam}} “I want to go”, both verbs say who: word for word “I want (that) I go”. And the second verb has a different form: not {{می‌روم}} but {{بروم|beravam}}.

blocks.means: a form of a verb for what is wanted, possible or needed rather than real: “(that) I go” in “I want to go”. In Persian it starts with {{بـ|be-}}.

blocks.p: **How to make it:** {{بـ|be-}} + the present stem + the ending you know. {{رو}} → {{بروم|beravam}} “(that) I go”; {{بین}} → {{ببینم|bebinam}} “(that) I see”; {{خر}} → {{بخرم|bekharam}}. Before a stem with an o in it, be- is said bo-: {{بخورم|bokhoram}} “(that) I eat”, {{بکنم|bokonam}}. Before {{آ}} it becomes {{بیا|biyâ}}: {{بیایم|biyâyam}} “(that) I come”.

**Compound verbs** usually have no {{بـ}}: {{می‌خواهم کار کنم.|mi-khâham kâr konam.}} “I want to work.” {{می‌خواهم با او صحبت کنم.|mi-khâham bâ u sohbat konam.}} “I want to talk to her.” A few keep it: {{یاد بگیرم|yâd begiram}} “learn”, {{زنگ بزنم|zang bezanam}} “call”.
**Not wanting.** “Not” goes on “want”: {{نمی‌خواهم بروم.|nemi-khâham beravam.}} “I don't want to go.”

ex.tr: I want to buy a car.
What do you want to eat?
We want to watch a film tonight.
She wants to become a doctor.
I don't want to work today.
Would you like to talk to the manager?

blocks.tip: In speech the subjunctive shrinks like the present: {{بروم}} is said {{برم|beram}}, {{بیایم}} {{بیام|biyâm}}, so you'll hear {{می‌خوام برم|mikhâm beram}} “I want to go”.

mistakes.why: After “want”, the second verb is in the subjunctive: {{بروم}}, with {{بـ}}.
Persian doesn't use the infinitive here: both verbs say who, “I want (that) I go”.

practice.tr: I want to go to Iran.
Do you want to come with me?

practice.q: A friend asks about your plans. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What do you want to do tomorrow?

lines.why: After {{می‌خواهم}}: {{بروم}}, the subjunctive.
“Do you want to come?”: {{می‌خواهی بیایی؟}}

practice.tr: I want to learn Persian.

practice.q: Say: “I don't want to work today.”
Your turn: say two or three things you want to do this year, with {{می‌خواهم}} and the subjunctive.

answers.t: می‌خواهم به ایران بروم و فارسی یاد بگیرم.
answers.r: mi-khâham be irân beravam va fârsi yâd begiram.
answers.tr: I want to go to Iran and learn Persian.

answers.t: می‌خواهم یک خانهٔ جدید بخرم.
answers.r: mi-khâham yek khâne-ye jadid bekharam.
answers.tr: I want to buy a new house.

answers.t: می‌خواهم بیشتر کتاب بخوانم و کمتر کار کنم!
answers.r: mi-khâham bishtar ketâb bekhânam va kamtar kâr konam!
answers.tr: I want to read more and work less!

lessons.title: Say what you can do, and ask if you may
lessons.summary: Say “I can swim”, “I can't come tomorrow”, and ask “May I sit here?” and “Could you speak more slowly?”
lessons.topic: {{توانستن}}: {{می‌توانم}} + subjunctive; {{نمی‌توانم}}; asking permission and favours; {{بلد بودن}}

goal.t: ببخشید، می‌توانم اینجا بنشینم؟
goal.r: bebakhshid, mi-tavânam injâ beneshinam?
goal.tr: Excuse me, may I sit here?

dialog.t: فردا شب می‌توانی بیایی؟ تولد مریم است.
dialog.r: fardâ shab mi-tavâni biyâyi? tavallod-e maryam ast.
dialog.tr: Can you come tomorrow night? It's Maryam's birthday.
I'm afraid I can't. I have to work.
What a shame! Can you on Saturday, then?
Yes, I can come on Saturday.

blocks.p: **Can.** {{می‌توانم|mi-tavânam}} “I can” (from {{توانستن|tavânestan}}, present stem {{توان|tavân}}) works just like {{می‌خواهم}}: the second verb is in the subjunctive. {{می‌توانم شنا کنم.|mi-tavânam shenâ konam.}} “I can swim.” {{می‌توانی بیایی؟|mi-tavâni biyâyi?}} “Can you come?”

**Asking permission:** {{می‌توانم … ؟}} “Can I…?, May I…?”: {{می‌توانم اینجا بنشینم؟}} “May I sit here?” ({{نشستن|neshastan}} “to sit”, present stem {{نشین|neshin}}). **Asking a favour:** {{می‌توانید … ؟}} “Could you…?”: {{می‌توانید کمکم کنید؟|mi-tavânid komakam konid?}} “Could you help me?”
**Knowing how.** For skills Persian also says {{بلد بودن|balad budan}} “to know how”: {{رانندگی بلدم.|rânandegi baladam.}} “I can drive.” {{شنا بلدی؟|shenâ baladi?}} “Can you swim?”

ex.tr: I can speak a little Persian.
I can't come tomorrow.
Could you speak more slowly?
Can I take photos here?

ex.t: او خیلی خوب می‌تواند آشپزی کند.
ex.r: u kheyli khub mi-tavânad âshpazi konad.
ex.tr: He can cook very well.
Could you help me?

blocks.tip: {{می‌توانید آهسته‌تر صحبت کنید؟}} and {{می‌توانید تکرار کنید؟|mi-tavânid tekrâr konid?}} “Could you say that again?” will be your two best friends in your first conversations.

mistakes.why: After {{می‌توانم}}, the subjunctive: {{بیایم}}.
“Can't” is on “can”: {{نمی‌توانم}}. ({{می‌توانم نیایم}} means “I'm allowed not to come”.)

practice.tr: Excuse me, may I sit here?
I'm afraid I can't come tomorrow.

practice.q: How do you ask someone, politely, to speak more slowly?
options: {{می‌توانید آهسته‌تر صحبت کنید؟|mi-tavânid âheste-tar sohbat konid?}}
{{می‌خواهم آهسته‌تر صحبت کنم.|mi-khâham âheste-tar sohbat konam.}}
practice.why: {{می‌توانید … ؟}} is “could you…?”. The other says “I want to speak more slowly.”

practice.q: A friend invites you. Choose your replies.

lines.t: جمعه می‌توانی بیایی؟ تولد مریم است.
lines.r: jom'e mi-tavâni biyâyi? tavallod-e maryam ast.
lines.tr: Can you come on Friday? It's Maryam's birthday.

lines.why: “I can't” is one verb: {{نمی‌توانم}}.
After {{می‌توانم}}: {{بیایم}}.

practice.tr: Can I take photos here?

practice.q: Ask a stranger politely: “Could you help me?”
Your turn: say two things you can do and one you can't, with {{می‌توانم}} and {{نمی‌توانم}}.

answers.t: می‌توانم شنا کنم، ولی نمی‌توانم رانندگی کنم.
answers.r: mi-tavânam shenâ konam, vali nemi-tavânam rânandegi konam.
answers.tr: I can swim, but I can't drive.

answers.t: می‌توانم کمی فارسی بخوانم و بنویسم.
answers.r: mi-tavânam kami fârsi bekhânam va benevisam.
answers.tr: I can read and write a little Persian.

lessons.title: Say what you have to do
lessons.summary: Say “I have to go”, “You mustn't smoke here” and “You don't have to pay”.
lessons.topic: {{باید}} + subjunctive; {{نباید}}; {{لازم است}} and {{لازم نیست}}; {{بهتر است}}

goal.t: ببخشید، باید بروم. فردا صبح زود کار دارم.
goal.r: bebakhshid, bâyad beravam. fardâ sobh zud kâr dâram.
goal.tr: Sorry, I have to go. I have work early tomorrow morning.

dialog.t: ببخشید، برای قطار مشهد کجا باید بلیت بخرم؟
dialog.r: bebakhshid, barâye ghatâr-e mashhad kojâ bâyad belit bekharam?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, where do I buy a ticket for the Mashhad train?

dialog.t: اینجا. ولی باید پاسپورتتان را نشان بدهید.
dialog.r: injâ. vali bâyad pâsportetân râ neshân bedahid.
dialog.tr: Here. But you have to show your passport.
Here you are. Do I have to pay now?

dialog.t: بله، ولی لازم نیست نقد بدهید. کارت هم قبول می‌کنیم.
dialog.r: bale, vali lâzem nist naghd bedahid. kârt ham ghabul mi-konim.
dialog.tr: Yes, but you don't have to pay cash. We take cards too.

blocks.p: **Must, have to, should.** {{باید|bâyad}} covers all three, and it never changes: no {{می}}, no ending. The person goes on the second verb, which is in the subjunctive: {{باید بروم|bâyad beravam}} “I have to go”, {{باید بروی|bâyad beravi}} “you have to go”, {{باید برویم|bâyad beravim}} “we have to go”.

**Mustn't, shouldn't:** {{نباید|nabâyad}}: {{اینجا نباید سیگار بکشید.|injâ nabâyad sigâr bekeshid.}} “You mustn't smoke here.” **Don't have to** is a different idea: {{لازم نیست|lâzem nist}} “it isn't necessary”: {{لازم نیست بیایی.|lâzem nist biyâyi.}} “You don't have to come.”

**Advice.** {{باید}} is also for advice, a little stronger than English “should”: {{باید این فیلم را ببینی!|bâyad in film râ bebini!}} “You must see this film!”. Softer: {{بهتر است|behtar ast}} “it's better (to)”: {{بهتر است استراحت کنی.|behtar ast esterâhat koni.}} “You'd better rest.”

ex.tr: I should exercise every day.
We have to be there at eight.
You mustn't be late.
You don't have to take your shoes off.
You must read this book!
What do I have to do?

blocks.tip: {{باید}} is the same for everyone, so only the second verb's ending tells you who: {{باید برود|bâyad beravad}} “he has to go”.

mistakes.why: {{باید}} never takes an ending; the second verb says who.
After {{باید}}, the subjunctive: {{بروم}}.

mistakes.right: لازم نیست پول بدهید، مجانی است.
mistakes.tr: You don't have to pay, it's free.
mistakes.why: {{نباید}} is “you mustn't”; “you don't have to” is {{لازم نیست}}.

practice.tr: Sorry, I have to go.
We have to be there at eight.

options: {{لازم نیست پول بدهید.|lâzem nist pul bedahid.}}

practice.q: At a museum ticket office. Choose your replies.

options: یک بلیت، لطفاً. می‌توانم عکس بگیرم؟
یک بلیت، لطفاً. می‌توانم عکس می‌گیرم؟

rs: yek belit, lotfan. mi-tavânam aks begiram?
yek belit, lotfan. mi-tavânam aks mi-giram?

lines.t: بله، ولی نباید از فلاش استفاده کنید.
lines.r: bale, vali nabâyad az flâsh estefâde konid.
lines.tr: Yes, but you mustn't use the flash.

options: چشم. کیفم را هم باید بدهم؟
چشم. کیفم را هم بایدم بدهم؟
lines.why: {{باید}} has no ending: {{باید بدهم}}.
rs: cheshm. kifam râ ham bâyad bedaham?
cheshm. kifam râ ham bâyadam bedaham?

practice.tr: You mustn't smoke here.

practice.q: Ask: “What do I have to do?”
Your turn: say two things you have to do this week, and one thing you don't have to do.

answers.t: باید به بانک بروم و به پدرم زنگ بزنم. لازم نیست شنبه کار کنم.
answers.r: bâyad be bânk beravam va be pedaram zang bezanam. lâzem nist shanbe kâr konam.
answers.tr: I have to go to the bank and call my father. I don't have to work on Saturday.

answers.r: bâyad barâye emtehân dars bekhânam.
answers.tr: I have to study for the exam.

lessons.title: Suggest and invite
lessons.summary: Say “Let's go to the cinema!”, “Shall we eat out?” and “How about Friday?”, and answer an invitation.
lessons.topic: {{بیا}} / {{بیایید}} + subjunctive “let's”; the subjunctive as a suggestion ({{برویم؟}}); {{چطور است … ؟}}; {{شاید}}

goal.t: بیا امشب به سینما برویم!
goal.r: biyâ emshab be sinamâ beravim!
goal.tr: Let's go to the cinema tonight!

dialog.tr: Are you doing anything tonight?
No, why?

dialog.t: بیا با هم بیرون شام بخوریم.
dialog.r: biyâ bâ ham birun shâm bokhorim.
dialog.tr: Let's eat out together.
Good idea! Where shall we go?

dialog.t: چطور است به آن رستوران ایرانی جدید برویم؟
dialog.r: chetowr ast be ân resturân-e irâni-ye jadid beravim?
dialog.tr: How about going to that new Iranian restaurant?
Great. At eight?

blocks.p: **Let's.** {{بیا|biyâ}} “come!” (to a friend) or {{بیایید|biyâyid}} (to several people, or politely), then the “we” subjunctive: {{بیا برویم!|biyâ beravim!}} “Let's go!”, {{بیایید شروع کنیم.|biyâyid shoru' konim.}} “Let's start.”

**Shall we?** The “we” subjunctive alone, as a question, is a suggestion: {{برویم؟|beravim?}} “Shall we go?”, {{کجا برویم؟|kojâ beravim?}} “Where shall we go?”, {{چه بخوریم؟|che bokhorim?}} “What shall we eat?”. It works for “I” too, as an offer: {{کمکت کنم؟|komakat konam?}} “Shall I help you?”

**How about…?** {{چطور است … ؟|chetowr ast …?}} “how is it (if)…?” + the subjunctive: {{چطور است فردا برویم؟|chetowr ast fardâ beravim?}} “How about going tomorrow?”. **Maybe:** {{شاید|shâyad}} + the subjunctive: {{شاید بیایم.|shâyad biyâyam.}} “I might come.”

**Answering.** Yes: {{باشد|bâshad}} “OK” (said {{باشه|bâshe}}), {{فکر خوبی است|fekr-e khubi ast}} “good idea”, {{حتماً|hatman}} “definitely”. No, kindly: {{ببخشید، نمی‌توانم.|bebakhshid, nemi-tavânam.}} “Sorry, I can't.” and {{دفعهٔ بعد|daf'e-ye ba'd}} “next time”.

table: {{چطور است فردا برویم؟|chetowr ast fardâ beravim?}}

ex.tr: Let's take a photo!
What shall we do today?
Shall I pour some tea?
It might rain tomorrow.

ex.t: چطور است جمعه به کوه برویم؟
ex.r: chetowr ast jom'e be kuh beravim?
ex.tr: How about going to the mountains on Friday?

ex.t: بیا دیگر در این باره صحبت نکنیم.
ex.r: biyâ digar dar in bâre sohbat nakonim.
ex.tr: Let's not talk about it anymore.
ex.note: “not” in the subjunctive: {{نـ}} in the place of {{بـ}}

lessons.title: Ask and tell people to do things
lessons.summary: Give and follow directions, offer a seat and ask politely: “Go straight on”, “Please sit down”, “Don't worry!”
lessons.topic: the imperative: {{برو}}, {{بروید}}; {{نرو}}; {{بفرمایید}} and {{لطفاً}}; directions

goal.t: مستقیم بروید، بعد به چپ بپیچید.
goal.r: mostaghim beravid, ba'd be chap bepichid.
goal.tr: Go straight on, then turn left.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the National Museum?

dialog.t: این خیابان را مستقیم بروید. سر چهارراه به راست بپیچید.
dialog.r: in khiyâbân râ mostaghim beravid. sar-e chahârrâh be râst bepichid.
dialog.tr: Go straight along this street. At the crossroads, turn right.
Is it far?

dialog.t: نه، ده دقیقه پیاده است. نگران نباشید!
dialog.r: na, dah daghighe piyâde ast. negarân nabâshid!
dialog.tr: No, it's ten minutes on foot. Don't worry!
Thank you very much!

blocks.means: the form of a verb for telling someone to do something: Go! Sit down!

blocks.p: **Do it!** The imperative is the subjunctive without its ending, for one friend: {{برو!|boro!}} “go!”, {{بخور!|bokhor!}} “eat!”; and with -id for several people, or politely: {{بروید|beravid}}, {{بخورید|bokhorid}}. You already know two: {{ببخشید}} “excuse (me)” and {{بفرمایید}}.
**Don't.** {{نـ}} in the place of {{بـ}}: {{نرو!|naro!}} “don't go!”, {{نگران نباش.|negarân nabâsh.}} “don't worry” (“don't be worried”).

**Politely.** The -id form already sounds polite; {{لطفاً|lotfan}} makes it more so: {{لطفاً بنشینید.|lotfan beneshinid.}} “Please sit down.” {{بفرمایید|befarmâyid}} is the all-purpose polite imperative: “here you are”, “come in”, “sit down”, “help yourself”, “go ahead”. For a favour, {{می‌توانید … ؟}} (lesson 20) is softer still.

**Directions.** {{مستقیم بروید|mostaghim beravid}} “go straight on”, {{به راست بپیچید|be râst bepichid}} “turn right”, {{به چپ بپیچید|be chap bepichid}} “turn left”, {{سر چهارراه|sar-e chahârrâh}} “at the crossroads”, {{بعد از بانک|ba'd az bânk}} “after the bank”.

ex.tr: Please, have a seat.
Please write your name here.
Wait a minute!

ex.t: نگران نباش، همه چیز درست می‌شود.
ex.r: negarân nabâsh, hame chiz dorost mi-shavad.
ex.tr: Don't worry, everything will be fine.
Don't go there, it's very crowded.
So tell me, how are you?
ex.note: {{بگو ببینم}} “say, let me see”: a friendly way to begin

blocks.tip: {{بفرمایید}} is the word you'll hear most in Iran: when someone opens a door for you, offers you tea, hands you something or invites you to speak. Answer with {{ممنون|mamnun}}, or {{خیلی لطف دارید|kheyli lotf dârid}} “you're very kind”.

mistakes.why: To one friend, no ending: {{برو}}. The -id form is for being polite, or for several people.
“Don't” takes the place of {{بـ}}: {{نـ}} + {{رو}}, {{نرو}}.

practice.tr: Please sit down.

lessons.title: Talk about the future
lessons.summary: Say what you're doing tomorrow and what's arranged, and understand the formal future of the news: the present for the future, {{قرار است}}, and {{خواهم رفت}}.
lessons.topic: the present for the future; {{قرار است}} + subjunctive; the formal future {{خواه}} + past stem ({{خواهم رفت}}), to recognise

goal.t: قرار است فردا ساعت ده همدیگر را ببینیم.
goal.r: gharâr ast fardâ sâ'at-e dah hamdigar râ bebinim.
goal.tr: We're meeting tomorrow at ten.

dialog.tr: What are you doing at the weekend?

dialog.t: جمعه به کرج می‌روم. قرار است خانوادهٔ دوستم را ببینم.
dialog.r: jom'e be karaj mi-ravam. gharâr ast khânevâde-ye dustam râ bebinam.
dialog.tr: On Friday I'm going to Karaj. I'm meeting my friend's family.
When are you coming back?
Saturday morning. I have class on Saturday.
Have a good time!

blocks.p: **The present for the future.** Whenever the time is clear, Persian uses the present for the future, as English does with “I'm going tomorrow”: {{فردا به کرج می‌روم.|fardâ be karaj mi-ravam.}} “Tomorrow I'm going to Karaj.” {{بعداً زنگ می‌زنم.|ba'dan zang mi-zanam.}} “I'll call later.” This is how most of the future is said.

**It's arranged: {{قرار است}}.** {{قرار|gharâr}} is “an arrangement”, and {{قرار است|gharâr ast}} + the subjunctive is “it's arranged that…, … is supposed to…”: {{قرار است ساعت ده بیاید.|gharâr ast sâ'at-e dah biyâyad.}} “He's supposed to come at ten.” {{قرار است}} never changes; the second verb says who.

**The formal future.** In writing and on the news you'll find a future made with {{خواه}} (the stem of “want”) + the endings + the **past** stem: {{خواهم رفت|khâham raft}} “I will go”, {{خواهد آمد|khâhad âmad}} “he will come”. This {{خواه}} has no {{می}}, and the main verb never changes. It sounds formal: in conversation, use the present.

ex.tr: Next year I'm going to Iran.

ex.t: قرار است ساعت هفت شام بخوریم.
ex.r: gharâr ast sâ'at-e haft shâm bokhorim.
ex.tr: We're having dinner at seven.

ex.t: قطار ساعت شش حرکت خواهد کرد.
ex.r: ghatâr sâ'at-e shesh harekat khâhad kard.
ex.tr: The train will leave at six.
ex.note: an announcement; in a compound verb {{خواه}} comes between the two words

ex.tr: Tomorrow will be sunny.
When are you coming back?
I'll let you know later.

blocks.tip: {{همدیگر را دیدن|hamdigar râ didan}} “to see each other” is the everyday “to meet up”. To wish someone a good time: {{خوش بگذرد!|khosh begozarad!}}

mistakes.why: The formal future is {{خواهم}} + the **past** stem, with no {{می}}: {{خواهم رفت}}.
{{قرار است}} never changes; {{بروم}} says “I”.

practice.q: A friend asks about tomorrow. The everyday way to say “I'm going to the bazaar” is…
options: {{فردا به بازار می‌روم.|fardâ be bâzâr mi-ravam.}}
{{فردا به بازار خواهم رفت.|fardâ be bâzâr khâham raft.}}

practice.tr: He's supposed to come at ten.
The train will leave at six.

practice.q: A friend asks about your weekend. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What are you doing at the weekend?

lines.why: The present does the future: {{می‌روم}}.

options: با برادرم. قرار است ساعت شش راه بیفتیم.
با برادرم. قرار است ساعت شش راه می‌افتیم.

rs: bâ barâdaram. gharâr ast sâ'at-e shesh râh biyoftim.
bâ barâdaram. gharâr ast sâ'at-e shesh râh mi-oftim.

practice.tr: Next year I'm going to Iran.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you're doing next weekend, and one thing that's already arranged, with {{قرار است}}.

answers.r: shanbe be khâne-ye mâdaram mi-ravam. gharâr ast bâ ham nâhâr bokhorim.
answers.tr: On Saturday I'm going to my mother's. We're having lunch together.
