lessons.title: Say what you did
lessons.summary: Say what you did yesterday, where you were and what you had: the simple past, made from the past stem.
lessons.topic: the simple past: past stem + endings (none for “he, she”); {{بودم}}, {{داشتم}}; {{دیروز}}, {{دیشب}}, {{پارسال}}

goal.t: دیروز به بازار رفتم و یک فرش خریدم.
goal.r: diruz be bâzâr raftam va yek farsh kharidam.
goal.tr: Yesterday I went to the bazaar and bought a carpet.

dialog.tr: Where were you yesterday?
I went to Tajrish bazaar.
What did you buy?

dialog.t: یک روسری و کمی میوه خریدم. بعد با مریم ناهار خوردیم.
dialog.r: yek rusari va kami mive kharidam. ba'd bâ maryam nâhâr khordim.
dialog.tr: A headscarf and some fruit. Then Maryam and I had lunch.
Did you have a good time?
Yes, a lot!

blocks.p: **The past is easy.** Take the past stem (the infinitive without its -an) and add the endings: {{رفت|raft}} + -am = {{رفتم|raftam}} “I went”. No {{می}}, no {{بـ}}. And for “he, she” there is **no ending at all**: {{رفت}} “he went, she went”.

**Why you learned two stems.** The past stem comes straight from the infinitive, so the past is the most regular tense of all: {{دیدن}} → {{دیدم|didam}} “I saw”, {{خوردن}} → {{خوردم|khordam}} “I ate”, {{آمدن}} → {{آمدم|âmadam}} “I came”, {{کردن}} → {{کردم|kardam}} “I did”.

**Was, had.** “Be” and “have” work the same way: {{بودم|budam}} “I was”, {{داشتم|dâshtam}} “I had”. {{دیروز خانه بودم.|diruz khâne budam.}} “I was at home yesterday.” {{یک گربه داشتیم.|yek gorbe dâshtim.}} “We had a cat.”
**When.** {{دیروز|diruz}} “yesterday”, {{دیشب|dishab}} “last night”, {{پریروز|pariruz}} “the day before yesterday”, {{هفتهٔ پیش|hafte-ye pish}} “last week”, {{پارسال|pârsâl}} “last year”.

ex.tr: I saw a good film last night.
She went to Germany last year.
I worked a lot last week.
Where were you yesterday?

ex.t: بچه که بودم، یک سگ داشتیم.
ex.r: bachche ke budam, yek sag dâshtim.
ex.tr: When I was a child, we had a dog.
ex.note: {{بچه که بودم}} “when I was a child”, word for word “child that I was”

ex.tr: They came home at seven.

blocks.tip: Two verbs whose presents look odd have perfectly regular pasts: {{گفتن}} “to say” → {{گفتم|goftam}} “I said” (present stem {{گو|gu}}), and {{شدن}} “to become” → {{شدم|shodam}} (present stem {{شو|shav}}).

mistakes.why: In the past, “he, she” has no ending: just the past stem, {{رفت}}.

mistakes.tr: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.
mistakes.why: For one finished action, the simple past has no {{می}}: {{رفتم}}. (With {{می}} it means “I used to go” or “I was going”: lessons 29 and 30.)

practice.tr: I went to the cinema yesterday.
practice.why: A finished action in the past: past stem + -am, {{رفتم}}.

practice.tr: He came at ten last night.
practice.why: “He, she” in the past: the past stem alone, {{آمد}}.

practice.q: A friend asks about your weekend. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What did you do on Friday?

lines.why: Friday is over: the past, {{رفتم}}.

lines.tr: Did you have a good time?

options: بله، خیلی! از کوه خیلی خوشم آمد.
بله، خیلی! کوه را خیلی خوشم آمد.
lines.why: The past of {{خوشم می‌آید}} is {{خوشم آمد}}, still with {{از}}.
rs: bale, kheyli! az kuh kheyli khosham âmad.
bale, kheyli! kuh râ kheyli khosham âmad.

practice.tr: Yesterday I went to the bazaar and bought a carpet.

practice.q: Ask a friend: “Where were you yesterday?”
Your turn: say three things you did yesterday.

answers.t: دیروز صبح ورزش کردم، بعد به کتابخانه رفتم و شب با خانواده‌ام شام خوردم.
answers.r: diruz sobh varzesh kardam, ba'd be ketâbkhâne raftam va shab bâ khânevâde-am shâm khordam.
answers.tr: Yesterday morning I exercised, then I went to the library, and in the evening I had dinner with my family.

answers.t: دیروز خیلی کار کردم و زود خوابیدم.
answers.r: diruz kheyli kâr kardam va zud khâbidam.
answers.tr: Yesterday I worked a lot and went to bed early.

lessons.title: Ask what someone did, and say what you didn't
lessons.summary: Ask “When did you arrive?” and “Did you call the airport?”, and say “I didn't see it” and “I came three days ago”.
lessons.topic: {{نـ}} + past ({{نرفتم}}); questions in the past; compound verbs in the past; {{پیش}} “ago”

goal.t: سه روز پیش رسیدم، ولی چمدانم نرسید!
goal.r: se ruz pish residam, vali chamedânam naresid!
goal.tr: I arrived three days ago, but my suitcase didn't!

dialog.tr: When did you arrive?
I arrived three days ago.
Why didn't you call me?

dialog.t: ببخشید! خیلی کار داشتم. چمدانم هم نرسید!
dialog.r: bebakhshid! kheyli kâr dâshtam. chamedânam ham naresid!
dialog.tr: Sorry! I was really busy. And my suitcase didn't arrive!
Oh no! Did you call the airport?
Yes, I called yesterday.

blocks.p: **Didn't.** {{نـ}} on the front: {{رفتم}} → {{نرفتم|naraftam}} “I didn't go”, {{دیدم}} → {{ندیدم|nadidam}} “I didn't see”, {{آمد}} → {{نیامد|nayâmad}} “he didn't come” (before {{آ}}, a y comes in).

**Questions** in the past are made as always: with the voice, or with a question word in the answer's place: {{رسیدی؟|residi?}} “Did you arrive?”, {{کی رسیدی؟|key residi?}} “When did you arrive?”, {{چه گفت؟|che goft?}} “What did he say?”
**Compound verbs** change only their verb part, and {{نـ}} goes on it: {{زنگ زدم|zang zadam}} “I called”, {{زنگ نزدم|zang nazadam}} “I didn't call”; {{کار کردی؟|kâr kardi?}} “Did you work?”

**Ago.** {{پیش|pish}} after the time: {{سه روز پیش|se ruz pish}} “three days ago”, {{دو سال پیش|do sâl pish}} “two years ago”, {{چند دقیقه پیش|chand daghighe pish}} “a few minutes ago”. {{قبل|ghabl}} works too: {{یک ماه قبل|yek mâh ghabl}} “a month ago”.

ex.tr: I didn't go to work yesterday.
Why didn't you come last night?
What did she say?
Have you seen my bag?
ex.note: word for word “didn't you see my bag?”

ex.t: دو سال پیش فارسی را شروع کردم.
ex.r: do sâl pish fârsi râ shoru' kardam.
ex.tr: I started Persian two years ago.
Did you have breakfast? No, I didn't have time.

blocks.tip: For something that has just happened, Iranians often use the simple past where English says “have”: {{رسیدم!|residam!}} “I'm here!” (“I've arrived”), {{فهمیدم.|fahmidam.}} “I get it.” (“I've understood”).

mistakes.why: “Not” is joined to the verb: {{نرفتم}}.
In a compound verb, {{نـ}} goes on the verb part: {{زنگ نزدم}}.
“Ago” comes after the time: {{سه روز پیش}}. ({{قبل از}} is “before”.)

practice.tr: I didn't call him yesterday.
practice.why: {{نـ}} on the verb part of {{زنگ زدن}}: {{نزدم}}.

practice.tr: I went to Iran three years ago.

practice.q: Your friend is back from a trip. Choose your questions.

lines.why: She has already arrived: the past, {{رسیدی}}.

lines.tr: I got in last night. I'm very tired.

lines.why: Asking about last night: the past, {{خوردی}}.

practice.tr: Why didn't you come last night?

practice.q: Your turn: say one thing you did last week and one you didn't, and when, with {{پیش}}.

answers.t: دو روز پیش به دیدن مادربزرگم رفتم، ولی به دوستم زنگ نزدم.
answers.r: do ruz pish be didan-e mâdarbozorgam raftam, vali be dustam zang nazadam.
answers.tr: Two days ago I went to see my grandmother, but I didn't call my friend.

answers.t: هفتهٔ پیش ورزش نکردم. خیلی کار داشتم.
answers.r: hafte-ye pish varzesh nakardam. kheyli kâr dâshtam.
answers.tr: I didn't exercise last week. I was very busy.

lessons.title: Tell a story in order
lessons.summary: Tell what happened, step by step: “First…, then…, when I got there…, and suddenly…”
lessons.topic: {{اول}}, {{بعد}}, {{آخرش}}; {{بعد از}} and {{قبل از}} + noun; {{وقتی}} + past; {{که}} for “when (suddenly)”; {{ناگهان}}

goal.t: وقتی به خانه رسیدم، دیدم که در باز است.
goal.r: vaghti be khâne residam, didam ke dar bâz ast.
goal.tr: When I got home, I saw that the door was open.

dialog.tr: What happened yesterday?

dialog.t: اول به بانک رفتم. بعد اتوبوس گرفتم و به دانشگاه رفتم.
dialog.r: avval be bânk raftam. ba'd otobus gereftam va be dâneshgâh raftam.
dialog.tr: First I went to the bank. Then I took the bus to the university.
And?

dialog.t: وقتی به دانشگاه رسیدم، دیدم که کیف پولم نیست!
dialog.r: vaghti be dâneshgâh residam, didam ke kif-e pulam nist!
dialog.tr: When I got to the university, I saw that my wallet wasn't there!
Oh no! Then what did you do?

dialog.t: به بانک برگشتم. کیفم آنجا بود!
dialog.r: be bânk bargashtam. kifam ânjâ bud!
dialog.tr: I went back to the bank. My wallet was there!

blocks.p: **Step by step.** {{اول|avval}} “first”, {{بعد|ba'd}} “then”, {{بعد از آن|ba'd az ân}} “after that”, {{آخرش|âkharash}} “in the end”: {{اول صبحانه خوردم، بعد دوش گرفتم.|avval sobhâne khordam, ba'd dush gereftam.}} “First I had breakfast, then I had a shower.”

blocks.means: a part of a sentence with its own verb: “when I got home” in “When I got home, I called my mother”.

blocks.p: **When.** {{وقتی|vaghti}} “when” + the past starts a clause; the main clause follows, after a comma: {{وقتی به خانه رسیدم، به مادرم زنگ زدم.|vaghti be khâne residam, be mâdaram zang zadam.}} “When I got home, I called my mother.”

**Before and after.** {{بعد از|ba'd az}} “after” and {{قبل از|ghabl az}} “before” + a noun: {{بعد از کلاس|ba'd az kelâs}} “after class”, {{قبل از شام|ghabl az shâm}} “before dinner”. (Before and after a whole clause come in unit 7.)

**And suddenly.** {{ناگهان|nâgahân}} is “suddenly”. Telling a story, Persian also likes a {{که}} after the first part, for “and just then”: {{به خانه رسیدم که تلفن زنگ زد.|be khâne residam ke telefon zang zad.}} “I'd just got home when the phone rang.”
**What you saw.** After {{دیدم که|didam ke}} “I saw that”, Persian keeps the tense of that moment: {{دیدم که در باز است.}}, word for word “I saw that the door **is** open”.

ex.t: اول به بازار رفتیم، بعد ناهار خوردیم.
ex.r: avval be bâzâr raftim, ba'd nâhâr khordim.
ex.tr: First we went to the bazaar, then we had lunch.

ex.t: بعد از کلاس با دوستانم قهوه خوردم.
ex.r: ba'd az kelâs bâ dustânam ghahve khordam.
ex.tr: After class I had coffee with my friends.

ex.t: وقتی او را دیدم، خیلی خوشحال شدم.
ex.r: vaghti u râ didam, kheyli khoshhâl shodam.
ex.tr: When I saw her, I was very happy.
Suddenly the power went off.

ex.t: به خانه رسیدم که تلفن زنگ زد.
ex.r: be khâne residam ke telefon zang zad.
ex.tr: I'd just got home when the phone rang.
In the end, everything turned out fine.

blocks.tip: {{چه شد؟|che shod?}} “What happened?” and {{بعد چه شد؟|ba'd che shod?}} “And then what happened?” keep a story going. To show you're listening: {{جدی؟|jeddi?}} “really?”, {{وای!|vây!}} “oh no!, wow!”.

mistakes.tr: After class I had a coffee.
mistakes.why: “After” is {{بعد از}}: both words, before the noun.
The story is in the past, so both clauses are: {{رسیدم}}, {{زنگ زدم}}.

practice.tr: First I had breakfast, then I had a shower.
practice.why: “First” is {{اول}}; the next step starts with {{بعد}}.

lines.r: nemi-dânam! vaghti be khâne residam, didam ke nist.
lines.tr: I don't know! When I got home, I saw it wasn't there.

practice.tr: After class I had coffee with my friends.

Your turn: tell a short story about something that happened to you, in three steps: {{اول}}…, {{بعد}}…, {{وقتی}}…

answers.t: اول یک تاکسی گرفتم و به فرودگاه رفتم. وقتی رسیدم، دیدم که پاسپورتم در خانه است!
answers.r: avval yek tâksi gereftam va be forudgâh raftam. vaghti residam, didam ke pâsportam dar khâne ast!
answers.tr: First I took a taxi to the airport. When I got there, I saw that my passport was at home!

answers.t: دیروز اول کار کردم، بعد با دوستم به سینما رفتیم. آخرش در یک رستوران شام خوردیم.
answers.r: diruz avval kâr kardam, ba'd bâ dustam be sinamâ raftim. âkharash dar yek resturân shâm khordim.
answers.tr: Yesterday I worked first, then my friend and I went to the cinema. In the end we had dinner in a restaurant.

lessons.title: Say what you have done
lessons.summary: Talk about experiences and results: “Have you ever been to Iran?”, “I've never had fesenjan”, “He hasn't come yet”.
lessons.topic: the present perfect: the participle ({{رفته}}) + the short “am, are” ({{رفته‌ام}}); {{تا حالا}}, {{هرگز}}, {{هنوز … نـ}}, {{تازه}}

goal.t: تا حالا به ایران رفته‌ای؟
goal.r: tâ hâlâ be irân rafte-i?
goal.tr: Have you ever been to Iran?

dialog.tr: Have you ever had fesenjan?
No, I've never had it. What is it?

dialog.t: یک خورش با گردو و انار است. امروز درست کرده‌ام!
dialog.r: yek khoresh bâ gerdu va anâr ast. emruz dorost karde-am!
dialog.tr: It's a stew with walnuts and pomegranate. I've made some today!

dialog.t: عالی! تا حالا غذای ایرانی زیاد نخورده‌ام.
dialog.r: âli! tâ hâlâ ghazâ-ye irâni ziyâd nakhorde-am.
dialog.tr: Great! I haven't had much Persian food so far.
Then help yourself!

blocks.p: **Have done.** The present perfect is for what has happened up to now: experiences, and results you can see now. {{رفته‌ام|rafte-am}} “I have gone, I've been”, {{دیده‌ای؟|dide-i?}} “have you seen?”.

blocks.means: a form of a verb used to build other tenses, like English “gone, eaten”. In Persian it is the past stem + -e: {{رفته|rafte}}.

blocks.p: **How to make it:** the participle (past stem + {{ه}}, said -e), then the short “am, are” of lesson 3, after a small gap: {{رفته‌ام|rafte-am}}, {{رفته‌ای|rafte-i}}, {{رفته است|rafte ast}}, {{رفته‌ایم|rafte-im}}, {{رفته‌اید|rafte-id}}, {{رفته‌اند|rafte-and}}. “Not”: {{نـ}} in front, {{نرفته‌ام|narafte-am}}.

**The words that go with it.** {{تا حالا|tâ hâlâ}} “ever, so far” (word for word “until now”); {{هرگز|hargez}} or {{هیچ‌وقت}} “never”, with a negative verb; {{هنوز … نـ|hanuz … na-}} “not yet”; {{تازه|tâze}} “just”; {{قبلاً|ghablan}} “before, already”.

**Simple past or perfect?** With a finished time, the simple past: {{پارسال به ایران رفتم.|pârsâl be irân raftam.}} “I went to Iran last year.” For “ever”, “never”, “not yet” and results, the perfect: {{هنوز به ایران نرفته‌ام.|hanuz be irân narafte-am.}} “I haven't been to Iran yet.”

ex.tr: Have you seen this film?
I've never been to India.
Ali hasn't come yet.
I've just arrived.
Have you been here before?
She has written three books.

blocks.tip: In speech, and often in writing, the {{است}} of “he, she” is dropped: {{علی هنوز نیامده.|ali hanuz nayâmade.}} And {{رفته‌ام}} is both “I have gone” and “I have been”: {{تا حالا به شیراز رفته‌ای؟}} “Have you ever been to Shiraz?”

mistakes.why: “Not yet” goes with the present perfect: {{نیامده است}}.

mistakes.tr: I went to Iran last year.
mistakes.why: With a finished time like “last year”, the simple past: {{رفتم}}.

practice.tr: Have you ever had fesenjan?
Ali hasn't come yet.

practice.q: Which one answers “When did you go to Shiraz?”
practice.why: A finished time, {{پارسال}} “last year”: the simple past.

practice.q: Getting to know someone. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Have you ever been to Iran?

options: نه، هنوز نرفته‌ام، ولی خیلی دوست دارم بروم.
نه، هنوز نرفتم، ولی خیلی دوست دارم می‌روم.
lines.why: “Not yet”: the perfect, {{نرفته‌ام}}; and after {{دوست دارم}} “I'd love (to)”, the subjunctive {{بروم}}.
rs: na, hanuz narafte-am, vali kheyli dust dâram beravam.
na, hanuz naraftam, vali kheyli dust dâram mi-ravam.

lines.why: The perfect: the participle {{خوانده}} + {{ام}}.

practice.tr: I've never been to India.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you've done in your life, and one you've never done.

answers.t: به ژاپن رفته‌ام و سوشی درست کرده‌ام، ولی هرگز اسکی نکرده‌ام.
answers.r: be zhâpon rafte-am va sushi dorost karde-am, vali hargez eski nakarde-am.
answers.tr: I've been to Japan and I've made sushi, but I've never been skiing.

answers.r: tâ hâlâ se bâr be irân rafte-am.
answers.tr: I've been to Iran three times so far.

lessons.title: Say what you used to do
lessons.summary: Talk about your childhood and old habits: “When I was a child, we used to go up north every summer.”
lessons.topic: the imperfect: {{می}} + past stem + ending ({{می‌رفتم}}) for habits in the past; {{بچه که بودم}}; {{قدیم‌ها}}

goal.t: بچه که بودم، هر تابستان به شمال می‌رفتیم.
goal.r: bachche ke budam, har tâbestân be shomâl mi-raftim.
goal.tr: When I was a child, we used to go up north every summer.

dialog.t: مادربزرگ، شما بچه که بودید، چه کار می‌کردید؟
dialog.r: mâdarbozorg, shomâ bachche ke budid, che kâr mi-kardid?
dialog.tr: Grandma, when you were a child, what did you use to do?

dialog.t: در یک روستای کوچک زندگی می‌کردیم. صبح‌ها به مدرسه می‌رفتم و بعد از ظهر‌ها به پدرم کمک می‌کردم.
dialog.r: dar yek rustâ-ye kuchak zendegi mi-kardim. sobh-hâ be madrese mi-raftam va ba'd az zohr-hâ be pedaram komak mi-kardam.
dialog.tr: We lived in a small village. In the mornings I went to school, and in the afternoons I helped my father.
Did you have a TV?

dialog.t: نه! شب‌ها پدرم برایمان قصه می‌گفت.
dialog.r: na! shab-hâ pedaram barâyemân ghesse mi-goft.
dialog.tr: No! In the evenings my father used to tell us stories.

blocks.p: **Used to.** For things that happened again and again in the past, Persian puts {{می}} on the simple past: {{رفتم}} “I went (once)” → {{می‌رفتم|mi-raftam}} “I used to go, I would go”. The endings are the past ones, with none for “he, she”: {{می‌رفت|mi-raft}}.

blocks.means: a past form for what went on, or happened again and again: “I used to go”, “I was going”. In Persian: {{می}} + the past stem + the ending.

blocks.p: **Not:** {{نمی}}, as in the present: {{نمی‌رفتم|nemi-raftam}} “I didn't use to go”. **Be and have** don't take {{می}} here: {{بودم}} and {{داشتم}} already cover long states: {{یک دوچرخه داشتم.|yek docharkhe dâshtam.}} “I had a bike.”

**When I was a child.** {{بچه که بودم|bachche ke budam}}, word for word “child that I was”, is how Iranians start a childhood memory. Also {{قدیم‌ها|ghadim-hâ}} “in the old days” and {{آن موقع|ân mowghe'}} “back then”.

ex.tr: In the old days people used to write a lot of letters.

ex.t: پدرم هر روز صبح روزنامه می‌خرید.
ex.r: pedaram har ruz sobh ruznâme mi-kharid.
ex.tr: My father used to buy a newspaper every morning.

ex.t: آن موقع در اصفهان زندگی می‌کردیم.
ex.r: ân mowghe' dar esfahân zendegi mi-kardim.
ex.tr: Back then we lived in Isfahan.

ex.t: بچه که بود، اصلاً سبزی نمی‌خورد.
ex.r: bachche ke bud, aslan sabzi nemi-khord.
ex.tr: As a child, he never used to eat vegetables.

ex.t: هر جمعه با پدربزرگم به پارک می‌رفتیم.
ex.r: har jom'e bâ pedarbozorgam be pârk mi-raftim.
ex.tr: Every Friday we used to go to the park with my grandfather.
Back then I had long hair!

blocks.tip: The {{می}} past is also polite, for wishes and requests: {{می‌خواستم بپرسم…|mi-khâstam beporsam…}} “I wanted to ask…” sounds softer than “I want to ask”.

mistakes.wrong: بچه که بودم، هر تابستان به شمال رفتیم.
mistakes.right: بچه که بودم، هر تابستان به شمال می‌رفتیم.
mistakes.tr: When I was a child, we used to go up north every summer.
mistakes.why: “Every summer” is a habit: the imperfect, with {{می}}.

mistakes.wrong: بچه که بودم، یک دوچرخه می‌داشتم.
mistakes.right: بچه که بودم، یک دوچرخه داشتم.
mistakes.tr: When I was a child, I had a bike.
mistakes.why: {{داشتن}} doesn't take {{می}} here: {{داشتم}} already means “I had”.

practice.t: بچه که بودم، هر روز فوتبال بازی ___.
practice.tr: When I was a child, I used to play football every day.
practice.why: A habit in the past: {{می}} + the past stem, {{می‌کردم}}.
practice.r: bachche ke budam, har ruz futbâl bâzi ___.

practice.why: {{می}} + the past stem {{رفت}}: a repeated past action.

practice.t: آن موقع در یک خانهٔ کوچک زندگی ___.
practice.tr: Back then we lived in a small house.
practice.why: A long-lasting state in the past: the imperfect, {{زندگی می‌کردیم}}.
practice.r: ân mowghe' dar yek khâne-ye kuchak zendegi ___.

practice.q: An old school friend remembers. Choose your replies.

lines.t: یادت است؟ هر روز با هم به مدرسه می‌رفتیم!
lines.r: yâdat ast? har ruz bâ ham be madrese mi-raftim!
lines.tr: Do you remember? We used to go to school together every day!

lines.why: “Always” is a habit: {{می‌رسیدیم}}.

options: راست می‌گویی! ولی حالا هر روز درس می‌خوانم.
راست می‌گویی! ولی حالا هر روز درس خواندم.
lines.why: “Now” is the present: {{می‌خوانم}}.
rs: râst mi-guyi! vali hâlâ har ruz dars mi-khânam.
râst mi-guyi! vali hâlâ har ruz dars khândam.

practice.tr: My father used to buy a newspaper every morning.

practice.q: Start a childhood memory: “When I was a child…”
Your turn: say two things you used to do as a child, and one thing you never used to do.

answers.t: بچه که بودم، هر روز با دوچرخه به مدرسه می‌رفتم، ولی هیچ‌وقت صبحانه نمی‌خوردم.
answers.r: bachche ke budam, har ruz bâ docharkhe be madrese mi-raftam, vali hich-vaght sobhâne nemi-khordam.
answers.tr: When I was a child, I used to cycle to school every day, but I never used to eat breakfast.

answers.t: تابستان‌ها در باغ پدربزرگم بازی می‌کردیم.
answers.r: tâbestân-hâ dar bâgh-e pedarbozorgam bâzi mi-kardim.
answers.tr: In the summers we used to play in my grandfather's garden.

lessons.title: Say what was happening
lessons.summary: Set the scene of a story: “I was cooking when the phone rang”, “It was raining and there were no taxis.”
lessons.topic: the imperfect for the background ({{باران می‌آمد}}); the past progressive {{داشتم می‌رفتم}}; {{داشتم … که …}}

goal.t: داشتم غذا درست می‌کردم که تلفن زنگ زد.
goal.r: dâshtam ghazâ dorost mi-kardam ke telefon zang zad.
goal.tr: I was cooking when the phone rang.

dialog.tr: Why are you late?

dialog.t: داشتم از خانه بیرون می‌آمدم که مادرم زنگ زد.
dialog.r: dâshtam az khâne birun mi-âmadam ke mâdaram zang zad.
dialog.tr: I was just leaving the house when my mother called.
And then?

dialog.t: بعد باران می‌آمد و تاکسی نبود. خیابان‌ها خیلی شلوغ بود.
dialog.r: ba'd bârân mi-âmad va tâksi nabud. khiyâbân-hâ kheyli sholugh bud.
dialog.tr: Then it was raining and there were no taxis. The streets were really busy.
Never mind. Come on, will you have some tea?

blocks.p: **The background.** The imperfect ({{می}} + past) also describes what was going on: the scene behind the events. {{باران می‌آمد.|bârân mi-âmad.}} “It was raining.” {{همه خسته بودند.|hame khaste budand.}} “Everyone was tired.” The events that happen in that scene are in the simple past: {{… که تلفن زنگ زد.}} “… when the phone rang.”

**Right in the middle of it.** To stress that something was in progress, Persian puts the past of {{داشتن}} before the imperfect: {{داشتم می‌رفتم|dâshtam mi-raftam}} “I was (just) going”. Both verbs take the ending: {{داشتی می‌خوردی|dâshti mi-khordi}} “you were eating”, {{داشت می‌خوابید|dâsht mi-khâbid}} “she was falling asleep”. It's very common in speech, and fine in writing. It has no negative: for “I wasn't working”, use the plain imperfect, {{کار نمی‌کردم}}.

**… when suddenly.** The event that cuts in follows with {{که}}: {{داشتم غذا درست می‌کردم که تلفن زنگ زد.}} Or start with {{وقتی}}: {{وقتی رسیدم، داشتند شام می‌خوردند.|vaghti residam, dâshtand shâm mi-khordand.}} “When I arrived, they were having dinner.”

table: {{داشتم می‌خوابیدم که زنگ زدی.|dâshtam mi-khâbidam ke zang zadi.}}
I was falling asleep when you called.

ex.t: وقتی به ایستگاه رسیدم، قطار داشت می‌رفت.
ex.r: vaghti be istgâh residam, ghatâr dâsht mi-raft.
ex.tr: When I got to the station, the train was leaving.

ex.t: داشتیم شام می‌خوردیم که برق رفت.
ex.r: dâshtim shâm mi-khordim ke bargh raft.
ex.tr: We were having dinner when the power went off.

ex.t: هوا سرد بود و برف می‌آمد.
ex.r: havâ sard bud va barf mi-âmad.
ex.tr: It was cold and it was snowing.
What were you doing?
I was talking to my friend.
The children were playing in the yard.

blocks.tip: {{داشتن}} does the same with the present: {{دارم می‌آیم!|dâram mi-âyam!}} “I'm coming (right now)!”, {{دارد باران می‌آید.|dârad bârân mi-âyad.}} “It's raining (at the moment).”

mistakes.wrong: داشتم رفتم که تلفن زنگ زد.
mistakes.right: داشتم می‌رفتم که تلفن زنگ زد.
mistakes.tr: I was leaving when the phone rang.
mistakes.why: After {{داشتم}}, the verb is in the imperfect, with {{می}}: {{می‌رفتم}}.
Both verbs take the same ending: {{داشتم می‌رفتم}}.

practice.t: داشتم غذا درست ___ که تلفن زنگ زد.

answers.r: diruz sâ'at-e shesh dâshtam be khâne mi-raftam ke dustam râ dar khiyâbân didam.

lessons.summary: Say “I got tired”, “It's over”, “I lost my key” and “Sorry I'm late!”: the two partners of Persian compound verbs, {{کردن}} and {{شدن}}.
lessons.topic: {{شدن}} “become, get” for what happens, {{کردن}} for what someone does: {{تمام شد}} / {{تمام کردم}}, {{گم شد}} / {{گم کردم}}; {{دیرم شد}}

blocks.p: **Do it, or it happens.** Many compound verbs come in pairs: with {{کردن}} someone does it; with {{شدن}} it happens, by itself or to someone. {{کار را تمام کردم.|kâr râ tamâm kardam.}} “I finished the work.” {{کار تمام شد.|kâr tamâm shod.}} “The work is finished” (“became finished”).

**Become, get.** {{شدن|shodan}} (present stem {{شو|shav}}) on its own is “become, get”: {{خسته شدم.|khaste shodam.}} “I got tired.” {{عصبانی شد.|asabâni shod.}} “He got angry.” {{هوا سرد شد.|havâ sard shod.}} “It got cold.” {{دکتر شد.|doktor shod.}} “She became a doctor.”

**It happened to me.** As with {{سردم است}} (lesson 18), a few use a possessive ending for the person: {{دیرم شد.|diram shod.}} “I'm late” (“my lateness happened”), {{حالم بد شد.|hâlam bad shod.}} “I felt ill.”
**What happened?** {{چه شد؟|che shod?}} is the {{شدن}} question for everything, and {{چه شده؟|che shode?}} “What's happened? What's wrong?”.

I lost my key.

blocks.tip: Pairs like these are why Persian needs so few verbs. Learn a new word like {{آماده|âmâde}} “ready” and you get two verbs free: {{آماده کردن}} “to get (something) ready” and {{آماده شدن}} “to get ready”.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.summary: Say “Tehran is bigger than Shiraz”, “the best restaurant in town” and “She's like her mother”.
lessons.topic: {{ـتر}} + {{از}} “-er than”; {{ـترین}} before the noun “the -est”; {{بهتر}}, {{بیشتر}}; {{مثل}}, {{به اندازهٔ}}

goal.t: تهران از شیراز بزرگ‌تر است، ولی شیراز قشنگ‌تر است.
goal.r: tehrân az shirâz bozorg-tar ast, vali shirâz ghashang-tar ast.
goal.tr: Tehran is bigger than Shiraz, but Shiraz is prettier.

dialog.t: این گوشی را ببینید. از آن یکی سبک‌تر است.
dialog.r: in gushi râ bebinid. az ân yeki sabok-tar ast.
dialog.tr: Look at this phone. It's lighter than that one.
But it's more expensive, isn't it?

dialog.t: بله، کمی گران‌تر است، ولی دوربینش خیلی بهتر است.
dialog.r: bale, kami gerân-tar ast, vali durbinash kheyli behtar ast.
dialog.tr: Yes, it's a bit more expensive, but its camera is much better.
Which is your cheapest phone?

dialog.t: این یکی. ولی آن یکی بهترین گوشی ماست!
dialog.r: in yeki. vali ân yeki behtarin gushi-ye mâst!
dialog.tr: This one. But that one is our best phone!

blocks.p: **Bigger, cheaper.** Add {{ـتر|-tar}} to the adjective, after a small gap: {{بزرگ|bozorg}} “big” → {{بزرگ‌تر|bozorg-tar}} “bigger”, {{ارزان|arzân}} “cheap” → {{ارزان‌تر|arzân-tar}} “cheaper”. “Than” is {{از|az}}, before what you compare with: {{تهران از شیراز بزرگ‌تر است.}} is, word for word, “Tehran from Shiraz bigger is”.

blocks.means: the form of an adjective that compares two things: bigger, more expensive. In Persian: the adjective + {{ـتر|-tar}}.

blocks.p: **The biggest.** {{ـترین|-tarin}}, and then the adjective goes **before** the noun, with no ezafe: {{بزرگ‌ترین شهر|bozorg-tarin shahr}} “the biggest city”, {{بهترین دوستم|behtarin dustam}} “my best friend”. “In …” is an ezafe on the noun: {{بزرگ‌ترین شهر ایران|bozorg-tarin shahr-e irân}} “the biggest city in Iran”.

**Good, better, best.** {{خوب|khub}} has its own forms: {{بهتر|behtar}} “better”, {{بهترین|behtarin}} “best”. {{بیشتر|bishtar}} “more” and {{کمتر|kamtar}} “less” also go with verbs: {{بیشتر کار می‌کند.|bishtar kâr mi-konad.}} “He works more.” Much bigger, a bit cheaper: {{خیلی|kheyli}} or {{کمی|kami}} before it, {{خیلی گران‌تر|kheyli gerân-tar}} “much more expensive”.

**Like, as … as.** {{مثل|mesl-e}} + ezafe is “like”: {{مثل مادرش است.|mesl-e mâdarash ast.}} “She's like her mother.” {{به اندازهٔ|be andâze-ye}} is “as … as”: {{به اندازهٔ برادرش قدبلند است.|be andâze-ye barâdarash ghadboland ast.}} “He's as tall as his brother.”

lessons.title: Say what hurts
lessons.summary: At the doctor's or the pharmacy: “My head hurts”, “I have a fever”, “What should I do?”
lessons.topic: {{سرم درد می‌کند}}: a possessive ending + {{درد کردن}}; {{تب دارم}}, {{سرما خورده‌ام}}; {{باید}} again

goal.t: سرم درد می‌کند و تب دارم.
goal.r: saram dard mi-konad va tab dâram.
goal.tr: I have a headache and a fever.

dialog.tr: Please, what's the problem?

dialog.t: از دیروز گلویم درد می‌کند و سرفه می‌کنم.
dialog.r: az diruz galuyam dard mi-konad va sorfe mi-konam.
dialog.tr: My throat has been hurting since yesterday, and I'm coughing.
Do you have a fever too?
Yes, a little. And I'm very tired.

dialog.t: سرما خورده‌اید. باید استراحت کنید و زیاد آب بخورید.
dialog.r: sarmâ khorde-id. bâyad esterâhat konid va ziyâd âb bokhorid.
dialog.tr: You've caught a cold. You should rest and drink plenty of water.
Do I need medicine too?

dialog.t: بله، این نسخه را به داروخانه ببرید.
dialog.r: bale, in noskhe râ be dârukhâne bebarid.
dialog.tr: Yes, take this prescription to the pharmacy.

blocks.p: **It hurts: “my head does pain”.** Persian says, word for word, “my head does pain”: the body part with a possessive ending, then {{درد می‌کند|dard mi-konad}}. {{سرم درد می‌کند.|saram dard mi-konad.}} “My head hurts, I have a headache.” {{دندانش درد می‌کند.|dandânash dard mi-konad.}} “He has toothache.” The verb is always “it”, because it's the head that hurts.
**After a vowel** (other than a final {{ه}}), the endings take a y: {{گلویم|galuyam}} “my throat”, {{پایت|pâyat}} “your foot”, {{پایش|pâyash}} “his foot”.

**I have a fever, I've caught a cold.** {{تب دارم|tab dâram}} “I have a fever”, {{سرفه می‌کنم|sorfe mi-konam}} “I'm coughing”, {{سرما خورده‌ام|sarmâ khorde-am}} “I've caught a cold” (word for word “I've eaten cold”!), {{حالت تهوع دارم|hâlat-e tahavvo' dâram}} “I feel sick”.

**What should I do?** The doctor's advice comes with {{باید}} (lesson 21): {{باید استراحت کنید.}} “You should rest.” {{نباید ورزش کنید.|nabâyad varzesh konid.}} “You mustn't exercise.” {{این قرص را روزی سه بار بخورید.|in ghors râ ruzi se bâr bokhorid.}} “Take this pill three times a day.”

ex.tr: I have a stomach ache.
I've had toothache since last night.
ex.note: Persian uses the present here: next lesson

ex.tr: The child has a fever.
I think I've caught a cold.
Do you have a pill for a headache?

ex.t: این شربت را بعد از غذا بخورید.
ex.r: in sharbat râ ba'd az ghazâ bokhorid.
ex.tr: Take this syrup after meals.

blocks.tip: When someone is ill you'll hear {{بلا دور باشد|balâ dur bâshad}} “may harm stay far away” and {{خدا بد ندهد|khodâ bad nadahad}} “God forbid (anything bad)”. Saying them back is kind.

mistakes.why: The head does the hurting, so the verb is “it”: {{می‌کند}}. The {{م}} on {{سر}} says whose head.
After a vowel, the ending takes a y in writing: {{پایم}}. ({{پام|pâm}} is how it's said in speech.)

lessons.title: Say how long and since when
lessons.summary: Say “I've lived here for two years” and “since last year”, and ask “How long have you been learning Persian?”
lessons.topic: the time + {{است که}} + present ({{دو سال است که اینجا زندگی می‌کنم}}); {{چند وقت است که … ؟}}; {{از … تا حالا}}; {{از وقتی که}}

goal.t: دو سال است که فارسی یاد می‌گیرم.
goal.r: do sâl ast ke fârsi yâd mi-giram.
goal.tr: I've been learning Persian for two years.

dialog.t: فارسی‌ات خیلی خوب است! چند وقت است که فارسی یاد می‌گیری؟
dialog.r: fârsi-at kheyli khub ast! chand vaght ast ke fârsi yâd mi-giri?
dialog.tr: Your Persian is very good! How long have you been learning?

dialog.t: ممنون! حدود دو سال است. از وقتی که با همسرم آشنا شدم.
dialog.r: mamnun! hodud-e do sâl ast. az vaghti ke bâ hamsaram âshnâ shodam.
dialog.tr: Thanks! About two years. Since I met my wife.

dialog.t: چند وقت است که در تهران هستی؟
dialog.r: chand vaght ast ke dar tehrân hasti?
dialog.tr: How long have you been in Tehran?

dialog.t: سه ماه است که اینجا هستم.
dialog.r: se mâh ast ke injâ hastam.
dialog.tr: I've been here for three months.
So you're a real Tehrani now!

blocks.p: **“It's two years that…”** For something that started in the past and is still going on, Persian says, word for word, “it is two years that I live here”: the length of time + {{است که}} + the **present**: {{دو سال است که اینجا زندگی می‌کنم.|do sâl ast ke injâ zendegi mi-konam.}} “I've lived here for two years.” English says “have been”; Persian keeps the present, because it is still true.

**How long?** {{چند وقت است که … ؟|chand vaght ast ke …?}} “how long is it that…?”: {{چند وقت است که اینجا کار می‌کنی؟|chand vaght ast ke injâ kâr mi-koni?}} “How long have you been working here?” Or with a unit: {{چند سال است که …؟|chand sâl ast ke …?}} “how many years…?”.

**Since.** {{از|az}} + a starting point, often with {{تا حالا|tâ hâlâ}} “until now”: {{از پارسال تا حالا اینجا هستم.|az pârsâl tâ hâlâ injâ hastam.}} “I've been here since last year.” Before a clause: {{از وقتی که|az vaghti ke}} + past, “since (the time when)”: {{از وقتی که آمدم، باران می‌آید.|az vaghti ke âmadam, bârân mi-âyad.}} “It's been raining since I arrived.”
**Over now.** For a time that has ended, the simple past, with no {{است که}}: {{دو سال در شیراز زندگی کردم.|do sâl dar shirâz zendegi kardam.}} “I lived in Shiraz for two years” (and then left).

table: {{دو سال است که اینجا هستم.|do sâl ast ke injâ hastam.}}
I've been here for two years.
{{چند وقت است که اینجا هستی؟|chand vaght ast ke injâ hasti?}}
How long have you been here?
{{از پارسال اینجا هستم.|az pârsâl injâ hastam.}}
I've been here since last year.
{{از وقتی که آمدم …|az vaghti ke âmadam …}}
{{دو سال آنجا بودم.|do sâl ânjâ budam.}}
I was there for two years.

blocks.p: **Him, her, it.** As an object, {{او|u}} “him, her” and {{آن|ân}} “it” take {{را}} like any particular object: {{او را دیدم.|u râ didam.}} “I saw him (her).” {{آن را خریدم.|ân râ kharidam.}} “I bought it.” For things, Persian often leaves “it” out altogether: {{خریدم.}} “I bought (it).”

**To him, for her.** After a preposition, the pronoun is either a word ({{به او|be u}} “to him”, {{با تو|bâ to}} “with you”, {{برای ما|barâye mâ}} “for us”) or, very often, one of the possessive endings of lesson 4: {{برایم|barâyam}} “for me”, {{برایت|barâyat}} “for you”, {{برایش|barâyash}} “for him, her”.

**On verbs, in speech.** Everyday speech also hangs these endings on verbs and on the noun of a compound verb: {{دیدمش|didamash}} “I saw him”, {{بخورش|bokhorash}} “eat it”, {{کمکت می‌کنم|komakat mi-konam}} “I'll help you”. You've met some already ({{کمکم کنید}}, {{درستش می‌کنم}}). In careful writing, use {{او را}} and {{آن را}}.

**Myself.** {{خود|khod}} + an ending: {{خودم|khodam}} “myself”, {{خودت|khodat}} “yourself”, {{خودش|khodash}} “himself, herself”: {{خودم درست کردم.|khodam dorost kardam.}} “I made it myself.” “Each other” is {{همدیگر|hamdigar}}, as in lesson 24.

lessons.title: Give reasons and say why
lessons.summary: Say why: “because I was ill”, “because of the rain”, “so I stayed home”, and “to learn Persian”.
lessons.topic: {{چون}} and {{برای اینکه}} “because”; {{به خاطر}} + noun; {{پس}}, {{به همین دلیل}} “so”; {{برای اینکه}} + subjunctive “in order to”

blocks.p: **Because.** {{چون|chon}} or {{برای اینکه|barâye inke}} + a whole clause: {{نیامدم، چون مریض بودم.|nayâmadam, chon mariz budam.}} “I didn't come because I was ill.” The reason can also come first: {{چون مریض بودم، نیامدم.}}

**Because of.** Before a noun, {{به خاطر|be khâter-e}}, with the ezafe: {{به خاطر باران|be khâter-e bârân}} “because of the rain”, {{به خاطر تو|be khâter-e to}} “because of you, for your sake”. In writing also {{به دلیل|be dalil-e}}.

**So.** {{پس|pas}} “so, then” and {{به همین دلیل|be hamin dalil}} “that's why, for this reason”: {{خسته بودم، به همین دلیل زود خوابیدم.|khaste budam, be hamin dalil zud khâbidam.}} “I was tired, so I went to bed early.”

**In order to.** {{برای اینکه|barâye inke}} + the **subjunctive** gives a purpose: {{برای اینکه فارسی یاد بگیرم، به ایران رفتم.|barâye inke fârsi yâd begiram, be irân raftam.}} “I went to Iran to learn Persian.” With an ordinary verb it means “because”; with the subjunctive, “so that”: the verb tells you which.

table: {{چون خسته بودم|chon khaste budam}} because I was tired
{{برای اینکه دیر شد|barâye inke dir shod}} because it got late
{{به خاطر باران|be khâter-e bârân}} because of the rain
{{پس زود رفتم|pas zud raftam}} so I left early

blocks.p: **I think.** {{فکر می‌کنم|fekr mi-konam}} “I think”, then what you think, with or without {{که|ke}} “that”: {{فکر می‌کنم که حق با شماست.|fekr mi-konam ke hagh bâ shomâst.}} “I think you're right.” “I don't think so”: {{فکر نمی‌کنم.|fekr nemi-konam.}} For something uncertain in the future, the subjunctive often follows: {{فکر می‌کنم فردا باران بیاید.|fekr mi-konam fardâ bârân biyâyad.}} “I think it'll rain tomorrow.”

**In my opinion.** {{به نظر من|be nazar-e man}} or {{به نظرم|be nazaram}} “in my view” (word for word “to my sight”). To ask: {{به نظر شما … ؟|be nazar-e shomâ …?}} “What do you think…?”, {{نظرت چیست؟|nazarat chist?}} “What's your opinion?”.

**Agree, disagree.** {{موافقم|movâfegham}} “I agree” and {{مخالفم|mokhâlefam}} “I disagree”: adjectives (“agreeing”, “opposed”) with the short “am”. With whom: {{با تو موافقم.|bâ to movâfegham.}} “I agree with you.” And {{حق با توست|hagh bâ tost}} “you're right” (word for word “the right is with you”).

**How sure.** {{مطمئنم که …|motma'enam ke …}} “I'm sure that…”, {{مطمئن نیستم|motma'en nistam}} “I'm not sure”, and {{شاید|shâyad}} + the subjunctive “maybe”: {{شاید حق با تو باشد.|shâyad hagh bâ to bâshad.}} “Maybe you're right.”

blocks.means: a clause that describes a noun and says which one you mean: “who lives upstairs” in “the neighbour who lives upstairs”.

blocks.p: **Which one?** To say which person or thing you mean, Persian adds {{ی}} (-i) to the noun, puts {{که|ke}} “who, which, that” after it, then the rest: {{کتابی که خریدم|ketâbi ke kharidam}} “the book (that) I bought”, {{مردی که آنجاست|mardi ke ânjâst}} “the man who's there”. The noun comes first, as in English.

**One word for who, which and that.** {{که}} is used for people and things alike, and it is never left out: English can say “the book I bought”, Persian can't drop {{که}}. After a final {{ه}} the -i is written {{ای}}: {{خانه‌ای که خریدیم|khâne-i ke kharidim}} “the house we bought”.

**With {{را}}.** When the noun is the object of the main verb, {{را}} comes after the noun and its -i, before {{که}}: {{کتابی را که خریدم خواندم.|ketâbi râ ke kharidam khândam.}} “I read the book I bought.”

**The pronoun that stays.** When the noun is “with”, “to” or “in” something inside the clause, Persian keeps a pronoun there: {{کسی که با او صحبت کردم|kasi ke bâ u sohbat kardam}} “the person I talked to” (word for word “the person that I talked with him”), {{شهری که در آن زندگی می‌کنم|shahri ke dar ân zendegi mi-konam}} “the city I live in”.

lessons.title: Say what happens before and after
lessons.summary: Connect events in time: “before I go to sleep”, “after we've eaten”, “until you tidy your room” and “as soon as I arrive”.

blocks.p: **Before: the subjunctive.** {{قبل از اینکه|ghabl az inke}} “before” is always followed by the subjunctive, whatever the time, because what comes after it hasn't happened yet: {{قبل از اینکه بخوابم|ghabl az inke bekhâbam}} “before I sleep”; and in the past too: {{قبل از اینکه برود، به من زنگ زد.|ghabl az inke beravad, be man zang zad.}} “Before he left, he called me.”

**After: the past.** {{بعد از اینکه|ba'd az inke}} “after” takes the simple past, even for the future: {{بعد از اینکه شام خوردیم، می‌رویم.|ba'd az inke shâm khordim, mi-ravim.}} “After we've had dinner, we'll go.”

**Until, so that.** {{تا|tâ}} + the subjunctive is “until” or “so that”: {{صبر کن تا بیایم.|sabr kon tâ biyâyam.}} “Wait until I come.” {{بلند صحبت کن تا بشنوند.|boland sohbat kon tâ beshenavand.}} “Speak up so that they can hear.” With a negative it means “until … has”: {{تا تمام نکنی، نمی‌روی.|tâ tamâm nakoni, nemi-ravi.}} “You won't go until you've finished.”
**As soon as.** {{همین که|hamin ke}} + the past, for one event, even in the future: {{همین که رسیدم، زنگ می‌زنم.|hamin ke residam, zang mi-zanam.}} “As soon as I arrive, I'll call.”

lessons.title: Tell what someone said
lessons.summary: Pass on messages and news: “She said she'd be late”, “He asked whether you were free”, “Mum asked me to buy bread”.
lessons.topic: {{گفت که}} + the tense they used; {{پرسید که آیا …}}; requests: {{گفت که}} + subjunctive ({{گفت بیایم}}); {{به من گفت}}

blocks.p: **Persian keeps the tense.** To report what someone said, Persian puts {{گفت که|goft ke}} “he said that”, then the words **in the tense they were said in**. Ali said “I'm not coming” → {{علی گفت که نمی‌آید.}} English moves the tense back (“he wasn't coming”); Persian doesn't. Only the person changes: Ali's “I” becomes “he”.
**To whom.** {{به من گفت|be man goft}} “he told me”, {{به او گفتم|be u goftam}} “I told him”. {{که}} can be left out: {{گفت فردا نمی‌آید.}}

**Asking.** {{پرسید|porsid}} “he asked” (from {{پرسیدن}}). With a question word, keep it, in its place: {{پرسید کجا زندگی می‌کنی.|porsid kojâ zendegi mi-koni.}} “He asked where you lived.” For yes-or-no questions, {{که آیا|ke âyâ}} “whether”: {{پرسید که آیا وقت داری.|porsid ke âyâ vaght dâri.}} “He asked whether you had time.”

**Requests** become the subjunctive: “Come!” → {{گفت که بیایم.|goft ke biyâyam.}} “He told me to come” (“he said that I come”). {{از من خواست که کمکش کنم.|az man khâst ke komakash konam.}} “She asked me to help her.”

blocks.means: the “if” part of a sentence: “if it rains” in “If it rains, we'll stay at home”.

blocks.p: **If.** {{اگر|agar}} “if” starts the condition; the result follows, after a comma. For something that may well happen, the condition is in the **subjunctive**: {{اگر باران بیاید|agar bârân biyâyad}} “if it rains”. The result is in the present (for the future) or the imperative: {{… در خانه می‌مانیم.}} “we'll stay at home”, {{… به من زنگ بزن.}} “call me”. For what is true now, the condition can simply be in the present: {{اگر خسته‌ای، بخواب.|agar khaste-i, bekhâb.}} “If you're tired, sleep.”

**Or the simple past.** Persian often puts a one-off condition in the simple past, even about the future: {{اگر باران آمد، به موزه می‌رویم.|agar bârân âmad, be muze mi-ravim.}} “If it rains, we'll go to the museum.” {{اگر علی را دیدی، سلام برسان.|agar ali râ didi, salâm beresân.}} “If you see Ali, say hello.” English says “if it rains” here, never “if it rained”.

**Be and have** in the subjunctive: {{باشم|bâsham}}, {{باشی}}, {{باشد}}… for “be”, and {{داشته باشم|dâshte bâsham}}, {{داشته باشی}}… for “have”: {{اگر پول داشته باشم، …|agar pul dâshte bâsham, …}} “if I have the money, …”.

**If not, unless.** {{اگر}} with a negative verb: {{اگر نیایی، ناراحت می‌شوم.|agar nayâyi, nârâhat mi-shavam.}} “If you don't come, I'll be upset.” And {{مگر اینکه|magar inke}} + subjunctive is “unless”.

blocks.p: **Not real, just imagined.** For a situation that isn't true, or isn't likely, Persian takes a step into the past, as English does: the condition in the **past** ({{اگر پول داشتم|agar pul dâshtam}} “if I had money”) and the result in the **imperfect**, {{می}} + past ({{سفر می‌کردم|safar mi-kardam}} “I would travel”). So {{می‌کردم}} is both “I used to do” and “I would do”: the sentence tells you which.

table: {{اگر پول داشته باشم،|agar pul dâshte bâsham,}}
{{سفر می‌کنم.|safar mi-konam.}} If I have money, I'll travel.
{{سفر می‌کردم.|safar mi-kardam.}} If I had money, I'd travel.
{{می‌آمدم.|mi-âmadam.}} If I'd known, I'd have come.

blocks.p: **If I were you.** {{اگر جای تو بودم|agar jâ-ye to budam}}, word for word “if I were in your place”: {{اگر جای تو بودم، می‌رفتم.|agar jâ-ye to budam, mi-raftam.}} “If I were you, I'd go.” With “be” the condition is just {{بودم}}, {{بودی}}…: Persian has no special “were”.

**Too late now.** For a past that didn't happen, everyday Persian uses the imperfect on **both** sides: {{اگر می‌دانستم، می‌آمدم.}} “If I'd known, I would have come.” Careful writing also uses the past perfect, the participle + {{بودم}}: {{اگر زود‌تر آمده بودی، او را می‌دیدی.|agar zud-tar âmade budi, u râ mi-didi.}} “If you had come earlier, you'd have seen her.”

lessons.title: Hope and wish
lessons.summary: Say “I hope you get better soon”, “I wish you could stay” and “If only you were here”, and the warm wishes Iranians say every day.
lessons.topic: {{امیدوارم (که)}} + subjunctive; {{کاش}} + past or imperfect ({{کاش اینجا بودی}}); everyday wishes ({{خسته نباشید}}, {{سفر به خیر}})

goal.t: امیدوارم زود‌تر خوب شوی.
goal.r: omidvâram zud-tar khub shavi.
goal.tr: I hope you get better soon.

blocks.p: **I hope.** {{امیدوارم|omidvâram}} “I'm hopeful” (the short “am” again), then the subjunctive, with or without {{که}}: {{امیدوارم که بیایی.|omidvâram ke biyâyi.}} “I hope you'll come.” {{امیدوارم حالت خوب باشد.|omidvâram hâlat khub bâshad.}} “I hope you're well.” “We hope” is {{امیدواریم|omidvârim}}.

**I wish, if only.** {{کاش|kâsh}} (or {{ای کاش|ey kâsh}}) + the past is a wish about now that isn't true: {{کاش اینجا بودی.|kâsh injâ budi.}} “I wish you were here.” {{کاش ماشین داشتم.|kâsh mâshin dâshtam.}} “I wish I had a car.” Other verbs take the imperfect: {{کاش می‌توانستم بمانم.|kâsh mi-tavânestam bemânam.}} “I wish I could stay.” For a past you'd change, the past perfect: {{کاش زود‌تر آمده بودم.|kâsh zud-tar âmade budam.}} “I wish I'd come earlier.”
**About the future**, {{کاش}} takes the subjunctive, like {{امیدوارم}}: {{کاش فردا هوا خوب باشد.|kâsh fardâ havâ khub bâshad.}} “I do hope the weather's good tomorrow.”

table: {{کاش فردا باران نیاید.|kâsh fardâ bârân nayâyad.}}
I do hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

blocks.p: **Everyday wishes.** Persian is full of little wishes, mostly subjunctives with “may…” understood: {{خسته نباشید!|khaste nabâshid!}} “may you not be tired” (to anyone who has been working), {{سفر به خیر!|safar be kheyr!}} “have a good trip!”, {{نوش جان!|nush-e jân!}} “enjoy your food!”, {{تولدت مبارک!|tavallodat mobârak!}} “happy birthday!”.

ex.tr: I hope your exam goes well.
I wish we had more time.

ex.r: ey kâsh fârsi râ zud-tar shoru' karde budam!
ex.tr: I wish I'd started Persian sooner!

blocks.tip: {{خسته نباشید}} is one of the most useful things you can learn: say it to a taxi driver as you pay, to a shop assistant, to your teacher. The answer is {{سلامت باشید|salâmat bâshid}} “may you be well”.

lessons.title: Say how sure you are
lessons.summary: Guess and suppose: “He must be tired”, “She may have left”, “It's possible that…”, “Maybe they've forgotten.”
lessons.topic: {{شاید}} and {{ممکن است}} + subjunctive; {{باید}} “must be”; the perfect subjunctive ({{رفته باشد}}) for the past; {{حتماً}}, {{احتمالاً}}

goal.t: تلفنش را جواب نمی‌دهد. شاید خوابیده باشد.
goal.r: telefonash râ javâb nemi-dahad. shâyad khâbide bâshad.
goal.tr: He's not answering his phone. Maybe he's fallen asleep.

dialog.r: sâ'at noh ast va rezâ hanuz nayâmade.
dialog.tr: It's nine and Reza still hasn't come.

dialog.tr: Then he must be very tired. He's worked all week.

blocks.p: **Maybe, possibly.** {{شاید|shâyad}} “maybe” and {{ممکن است|momken ast}} “it's possible (that)” take the subjunctive: {{شاید بیاید.|shâyad biyâyad.}} “He might come.” {{ممکن است دیر برسیم.|momken ast dir beresim.}} “We may be late.”
**Must be.** {{باید}} also means “must be”, for a confident guess: {{باید خسته باشد.|bâyad khaste bâshad.}} “She must be tired.” {{باید ایرانی باشد.|bâyad irâni bâshad.}} “He must be Iranian.”

blocks.means: the subjunctive of the perfect, for what may (or must) have happened: {{رفته باشد|rafte bâshad}} “(that) he has gone”.

blocks.p: **Guessing about the past.** Use the participle + the subjunctive of “be” ({{باشم}}, {{باشی}}, {{باشد}}…): {{شاید رفته باشد.|shâyad rafte bâshad.}} “Maybe he's gone, he may have gone.” {{باید فراموش کرده باشد.|bâyad farâmush karde bâshad.}} “She must have forgotten.”

table: {{شاید آمده باشد.|shâyad âmade bâshad.}} He may have come.
{{ممکن است بداند.|momken ast bedânad.}} She may know.
{{ممکن است شنیده باشد.|momken ast shenide bâshad.}} She may have heard.
{{باید خانه باشد.|bâyad khâne bâshad.}} He must be home.
{{باید رفته باشد.|bâyad rafte bâshad.}} He must have left.

blocks.p: **Sure and probable.** {{حتماً|hatman}} “surely, definitely”, {{احتمالاً|ehtemâlan}} “probably” and {{مطمئناً|motma'ennan}} “certainly” go with ordinary verbs: {{احتمالاً فردا می‌آید.|ehtemâlan fardâ mi-âyad.}} “He'll probably come tomorrow.”

ex.tr: It might snow tonight.
You must be very hungry!

ex.tr: I'll probably call you tomorrow.

blocks.tip: {{باید}} has two jobs: “have to” ({{باید بروم}} “I have to go”) and “must be” ({{باید خسته باشد}} “she must be tired”). The situation tells you which.

lessons.title: Be polite the Persian way
lessons.summary: Offer, accept and refuse like an Iranian: ta'ârof, the respectful plural, and the special polite verbs.
lessons.topic: ta'ârof phrases ({{بفرمایید}}, {{خواهش می‌کنم}}, {{قابلی ندارد}}); {{شما}} and {{ایشان}} with a plural verb; polite verbs ({{تشریف آوردن}}, {{میل کردن}}, {{فرمودن}})

goal.t: خیلی خوش آمدید، بفرمایید بنشینید.
goal.r: kheyli khosh âmadid, befarmâyid beneshinid.

blocks.p: **Ta'ârof.** Iranian politeness is a small ritual called {{تعارف|ta'ârof}}: offering again and again, refusing at first, and lowering yourself while raising the other person. A taxi driver or a shopkeeper may say {{قابلی ندارد|ghâbeli nadârad}}, “it's not worthy (of you)”, as if you needn't pay. It's courtesy: insist kindly, and pay.

**Offers.** The host offers ({{بفرمایید|befarmâyid}}); the guest refuses politely ({{ممنون، میل ندارم|mamnun, meyl nadâram}} “thank you, I don't feel like it”, {{زحمت نکشید|zahmat nakeshid}} “don't go to any trouble”); the host insists ({{تعارف نکنید!|ta'ârof nakonid!}} “don't stand on ceremony!”); and then the guest accepts. If you really mean no, say it more than once.

**Respect: the plural.** {{شما|shomâ}} takes a plural verb even for one person. For a respected “he” or “she” (a teacher, someone older), Persian uses {{ایشان|ishân}}, also with a plural verb: {{ایشان استاد من هستند.|ishân ostâd-e man hastand.}} “She is my professor.”

**Polite verbs.** Some verbs have a special polite form, for the other person, never for yourself: {{تشریف آوردن|tashrif âvardan}} “to come” ({{کی تشریف آوردید؟|key tashrif âvardid?}} “when did you arrive?”), {{تشریف بردن|tashrif bordan}} “to go”, {{میل کردن|meyl kardan}} “to eat, to drink” ({{چه میل دارید؟}}), {{فرمودن|farmudan}} “to say” ({{چه فرمودید؟|che farmudid?}} “what did you say?”). About yourself, humble words: {{عرض کردم|arz kardam}} “I said”.

ex.tr: Please come in!
Please don't go to any trouble, thank you.
Don't be shy, help yourself!
Sorry, what did you say?
You're very kind.
Is your father in?
ex.note: on the phone or at the door

blocks.tip: Two answers you'll use a hundred times: to thanks, {{خواهش می‌کنم|khâhesh mi-konam}} “you're welcome” (word for word “I beg you”); to a compliment, {{لطف دارید|lotf dârid}} or {{نظر لطف شماست|nazar-e lotf-e shomâst}} “that's your kindness”.

mistakes.why: Polite verbs are for the other person, never for yourself: about yourself, {{آمدم}}.
For someone you respect, the plural verb: {{آمدند}} (politer still, {{تشریف آوردند}}).

blocks.means: a sentence that puts the thing done first and leaves out the doer, or brings it in later: “The mosque was built.”

blocks.p: **Things that are done.** When what matters is what happened, not who did it, Persian uses the **passive**: the participle + {{شدن}}. {{ساخته شد|sâkhte shod}} “it was built” (from {{ساختن}} “to build”), {{گفته می‌شود|gofte mi-shavad}} “it is said”, {{نوشته شده است|neveshte shode ast}} “it has been written”. Only {{شدن}} changes tense.
**By whom.** In writing, {{توسط|tavassot-e}} “by”: {{این نامه توسط مدیر نوشته شد.|in nâme tavassot-e modir neveshte shod.}} “This letter was written by the manager.”

**Compound verbs** with {{کردن}} make their passive by swapping in {{شدن}} (lesson 31): {{درست کرد}} “he made (it)” → {{درست شد}} “it was made”; {{ترجمه کردند}} “they translated” → {{ترجمه شد}} “it was translated”.

**In speech**, Persian prefers “they”: {{می‌گویند|mi-guyand}} “they say” rather than {{گفته می‌شود}}; {{اینجا انگلیسی صحبت می‌کنند.|injâ engelisi sohbat mi-konand.}} “English is spoken here” (“they speak English here”).

lessons.title: Follow everyday spoken Persian
lessons.summary: Recognise how Iranians really talk: the same grammar, in shorter sounds ({{می‌رم}} for {{می‌روم}}, {{خونه}} for {{خانه}}, {{خوبه}} for {{خوب است}}).
lessons.topic: the spoken forms of the written standard: shorter verbs ({{می‌رم}}, {{می‌خوام}}), â before n said u ({{خونه}}), {{است}} → -e, {{را}} → -o, endings on verbs

goal.t: نمی‌توانم بیایم، کار دارم.
goal.r: nemi-tavânam biyâyam, kâr dâram.
goal.tr: I can't come, I'm busy.
goal.note: said: {{نمی‌تونم بیام، کار دارم.|nemitunam biyâm, kâr dâram.}}

blocks.p: **Same grammar, shorter sounds.** Everything in this course is the standard Persian of writing, the news and careful speech. In everyday conversation (in Tehran, and on Iranian TV and film) people say many words in shorter forms, a bit like English “gonna” and “wanna”. There is no new grammar here: this lesson is for recognising them.
**â before n is said u.** {{خانه}} khâne is said khune, {{نان}} nân nun, {{آن}} ân un, {{تهران}} tehrân tehrun, {{می‌دانم}} mi-dânam midunam, {{می‌توانم}} mi-tavânam mitunam.

**Verbs get shorter.** {{می‌روم}} → miram, {{می‌گویم}} → migam, {{می‌خواهم}} → mikhâm, {{می‌آیم}} → miyâm, {{بروم}} → beram. {{است}} becomes -e after a consonant ({{خوب است}} → khube) and disappears after a vowel. “They” loses its d: {{می‌روند}} → miran.

**Endings everywhere.** Speech hangs the pronoun endings on verbs and prepositions (lesson 35): {{دیدمش|didamesh}} “I saw him”, {{بهش گفتم|behesh goftam}} “I told him”, {{ازت ممنونم|azat mamnunam}} “thank you” (“I'm grateful to you”). And {{هم}} “too” shrinks to -am: {{منم|manam}} “me too”.

ex.tr: I don't know where it is.
This is really good!
I want to go home.

ex.tr: What are you saying?

blocks.tip: When you speak, the standard forms are always understood and always polite: use the spoken ones as you start to hear them. Don't write them, except in chats with friends.

mistakes.why: In writing (an email, a form, a letter), use the standard forms; the spoken ones are for talk and friendly chat.
Written, {{را}} is always {{را}}, and {{خواندم}} keeps its {{ا}}.

{{از خانه می‌آیم.|az khâne mi-âyam.}} I'm coming from home.

lessons.title: Tell your story: past, present and future
lessons.summary: Put it all together: who you are, where you've been, what you're doing now and what you hope for.
lessons.topic: every tense together: the past, the imperfect, the perfect, the present, the subjunctive and conditions

goal.t: سه سال پیش فارسی را شروع کردم، الان می‌توانم با دوستانم صحبت کنم و امیدوارم یک روز به ایران بروم.
goal.r: se sâl pish fârsi râ shoru' kardam, al'ân mi-tavânam bâ dustânam sohbat konam va omidvâram yek ruz be irân beravam.
goal.tr: I started Persian three years ago, now I can talk with my friends, and I hope to go to Iran one day.

dialog.tr: Tell me a little about yourself.

dialog.t: من اهل کانادا هستم. پنج سال است که در تهران زندگی می‌کنم.
dialog.r: man ahl-e kânâdâ hastam. panj sâl ast ke dar tehrân zendegi mi-konam.
dialog.tr: I'm from Canada. I've lived in Tehran for five years.
Where did you work before?

dialog.t: در یک مدرسهٔ زبان درس می‌دادم. آنجا خیلی چیز‌ها یاد گرفتم.
dialog.r: dar yek madrese-ye zabân dars mi-dâdam. ânjâ kheyli chiz-hâ yâd gereftam.
dialog.tr: I taught at a language school. I learned a lot there.
Why do you want to work here?

dialog.t: چون شرکت شما را می‌شناسم و فکر می‌کنم که می‌توانم کمک کنم. اگر این کار را بگیرم، خیلی خوشحال می‌شوم.
dialog.r: chon sherkat-e shomâ râ mi-shenâsam va fekr mi-konam ke mi-tavânam komak konam. agar in kâr râ begiram, kheyli khoshhâl mi-shavam.
dialog.tr: Because I know your company and I think I can help. If I get this job, I'll be very happy.

blocks.p: **Everything you've learned, in one story.** Telling your story uses every tense in the course: who you are (“be”), what happened (the past), what you used to do (the imperfect), what you've done (the perfect), what you do now and for how long (the present), and what you want, hope and would do (the subjunctive and conditions).

blocks.p: **Link it.** The joining words of unit 7 make it flow: {{اول}}, {{بعد}}, {{وقتی}}, {{چون}}, {{برای اینکه}}, {{ولی}}, {{به همین دلیل}}. And a story sounds natural when its scenes have a background (the imperfect) and events (the past).

ex.t: در یک شهر کوچک به دنیا آمدم و بچه که بودم، هر تابستان به خانهٔ مادربزرگم می‌رفتم.
ex.r: dar yek shahr-e kuchak be donyâ âmadam va bachche ke budam, har tâbestân be khâne-ye mâdarbozorgam mi-raftam.
ex.tr: I was born in a small town, and as a child I used to go to my grandmother's every summer.

ex.t: بعد از دانشگاه، دو سال در آلمان کار کردم.
ex.r: ba'd az dâneshgâh, do sâl dar âlmân kâr kardam.
ex.tr: After university, I worked in Germany for two years.

ex.t: تا حالا به ده کشور سفر کرده‌ام، ولی هنوز به ایران نرفته‌ام.
ex.r: tâ hâlâ be dah keshvar safar karde-am, vali hanuz be irân narafte-am.
ex.tr: I've been to ten countries so far, but I haven't been to Iran yet.

ex.t: الان معلم هستم و سه سال است که فارسی یاد می‌گیرم.
ex.r: al'ân mo'allem hastam va se sâl ast ke fârsi yâd mi-giram.
ex.tr: Now I'm a teacher, and I've been learning Persian for three years.

ex.t: می‌خواهم سال دیگر به اصفهان بروم، چون می‌خواهم میدان نقش جهان را ببینم.
ex.r: mi-khâham sâl-e digar be esfahân beravam, chon mi-khâham meydân-e naghsh-e jahân râ bebinam.
ex.tr: I want to go to Isfahan next year, because I want to see Naqsh-e Jahan Square.

ex.t: اگر پول داشتم، یک خانهٔ کوچک در شمال می‌خریدم.
ex.r: agar pul dâshtam, yek khâne-ye kuchak dar shomâl mi-kharidam.
ex.tr: If I had the money, I'd buy a little house up north.
